The restriction exists because a non-value global is a pointer slot whose target's lifetime is the module's, so rebinding needs an ownership story for the old value and storage for the new one; deciding that story is the work. Surfaced by a downstream port.
- **Methods on enums -- deferred slices** (shipped: instance / `@property` / `@staticmethod` / `@classmethod` on `Enum` and `IntEnum`, as ordinary methods of the companion record `__enum_<Name>`, which wraps the member by value -- see LANGUAGE_FEATURES and ENUM_DESIGN "Methods"). Each slice is a located error today, never silent. (1) **Dunders**: a per-member `__str__`/`__repr__` needs the enum's `operator<<` to route to the companion; `__eq__`/ordering/`__bool__`/`__hash__` would otherwise render the intrinsic enum operator silently (a user dunder's `cpp_template` is operator syntax), so they need the comparison, truthiness and hashing arms to consult the companion before the intrinsic rule. (2) **`_missing_`**: `Color(99)` consults it in CPython; the companion's classmethod would be the fallback arm of `EnumUtil<E>::from_value`. (3) **Generator and `async` methods**: the resumable frame borrows a method's receiver through `this`, and an enum call's companion wrapper is a temporary, so the frame must hold the member by value instead (unprobed). (4) **Nested enums**: the companion would nest inside the outer record; unprobed. (5) **`@export` enums**: the CPython side is a bare recreated IntEnum/Enum, so the methods would be missing; exposing them needs METH glue on the recreated type (or a `PyType_FromSpec` enum). (6) **A method as a value** (`f = Color.label`, `g = c.label`): rejected with its own message; the same gap as a record's bound method. (7) **Unbound call through the type** (`Color.label(c)`): rejected exactly as `Point.norm(p)` is for a record; lifting it for records lifts it here. (8) **Structural protocol conformance**: an enum with methods never satisfies a structural `Protocol` ("does not conform"; CPython duck-types it). Conformance would need the check to consult `receiver_record`, and the monomorphized call to render through the companion wrapper rather than `x.m()` on the enum.
- **[low prio] Lift the fixed receiver-NAME requirement for `self` / `cls`.** The parser rejects any instance method whose first parameter is not spelled `self`, and any `@classmethod` whose first is not `cls` (`_parse_method`, plus the protocol-method branch). Python enforces neither -- it binds the first positional parameter whatever its name is, and PEP 8 only *recommends* `self`/`cls` -- so `def make(klass)` / `def __new__(mcs, ...)` is valid Python that TPy rejects. Loud and located, never silent, and PEP 8-conformant code never hits it, which is why this is low priority rather than a bug. Realistic reachers: metaclass-style code using `mcs`/`mcls`, and machine-generated or ported sources. The work is to stop keying on the literal string: the parser already computes a `receiver_name`, so thread it as a fact into (a) the sema binding, registered today as `NameBinding(kind=RECORD, name="cls", ...)` in `sema/analyzer.py`, (b) the rebind guard `_check_cls_not_rebound`, which string-matches `"cls"` across every binder form, and (c) the value-read diagnostic in `sema/expressions.py`, which special-cases `expr.name == "cls"`. The `self` half additionally touches whatever reads the `self` binding by name. Note the interaction with the rebind guard: a user-chosen receiver name that collides with a module-level record name would have hit the Namespace-before-Scope precedence bug, which is now fixed for the three `as`-capture forms -- so the guard's conservatism can be revisited on its own merits rather than blocked on that. Surfaced reviewing why `error_first_param_not_cls` rejects valid Python.
- **`@classmethod` v1 exclusions** (shipped: `cls` bound to the DEFINING class -- see LANGUAGE_FEATURES). Each is a located error today, not a silent gap: (1) **`cls` as a value** (`return cls`, `f(cls)`, `isinstance(x, cls)`) -- needs `type[T]`; same prerequisite as polymorphic `cls`, tracked as the `type[Self]` row in FEATURE_ROADMAP Future Extensions. (2) **nested classes** -- a nested record is renamed `Outer.Inner` after parsing and has no bare-name spelling for `cls` to resolve to; the fix is to normalize `cls` to the field-access receiver shape the user would write. (3) **in a `Protocol` body** -- blocked on the sibling gap below (`@staticmethod` is rejected there too). (4) **on a `@native` record as a `...` stub** -- unverified rather than rejected; a BODIED method on a `@native` class is already rejected ("must have '...' body"), so only the degenerate stub form (where `cls` has no body to bind in) is unexplored. (5) **across the `@export` CPython boundary** -- needs `METH_CLASS` glue, already tracked as static/classmethods (item 5) in the CPython-interop entry.
- **Revisit the `cls`-rebind parser rejects now that capture registration is fixed.** The parser rejects every form that rebinds `cls` (`except/case ... as cls`, `import x as cls`, a comprehension target named `cls`) because a capture used to be invisible to name resolution, so the read silently hit the class. That shadowing bug is fixed for the three capture forms, so the except/case rejects can relax to ordinary shadowing. The COMPREHENSION reject needs its own analysis and does NOT follow from the fix: comprehension targets were never affected by the shadowing bug (verified -- they bind the namespace correctly and do not leak past the comprehension), so the real question there is whether a target named `cls` would OVERWRITE the `is_sema_alias` RECORD binding in the method local namespace, a different mechanism. The rationale comment in `tests/cases/classmethod/error_cls_rebind_comprehension/src/main.py` states the old (wrong) reason and should be corrected with whatever the analysis concludes.
- **Unify the "resolve a construction's record" fallback across the AST and THIR mirrors.** `get_record(callee_spelling)`, else the sema result type via `get_expr_type` -> `NominalType` -> `get_record_for_type`, is now spelled near-verbatim in `codegen_cpp/expressions.py` (the record-ctor branch) and `thir/lower/checks.py::_ctor_shape_ok` -- two phase mirrors that must stay in lockstep. The sibling decision for STATIC CALLS was unified properly into one shared helper (`codegen_cpp/context.py::static_method_callee_cpp`, threaded an `owner`), so the asymmetry is just unfinished: extract the ctor fallback the same way (a registry method beside `get_record`/`get_record_for_type` is the natural home). The sibling iterable-lvalue family was unified exactly like this -- one `is_constructor_call` in `codegen_cpp/context.py` consumed by the AST arm and both THIR mirrors -- after the third copy turned out to be the one carrying a bug; follow that shape. Surfaced by /tpy-review (architecture-fit) on the classmethod branch.
- **`@staticmethod` / `@classmethod` in a `Protocol` body is rejected** (`Unknown decorator 'staticmethod' on protocol method`, `_parse_class`'s protocol branch). This blocks a *constructor requirement* in a protocol -- the `ConstructibleFromRange.from_range(cls, items) -> Self` shape `docs/PROTOCOL_DESIGN.md` itself sketches as a built-in trait. Structural conformance would need to match static members (`T::from_range(...)` in the concept) rather than instance methods; a genuinely useful version also wants polymorphic `cls`, so the two are best designed together.
- **Widen `__init__` field auto-declaration past a bare parameter RHS (`self.count = 0` is the first wall a new user hits).** Today a field is auto-declared ONLY when the assigned expression is a bare parameter name: `self.total = start` works, but `self.count = 0`, `self.c = p * 2.0`, `self.c = g()`, `self.c = []` and every other RHS error `Record 'A' has no field 'count'` and require a class-level annotation. This is *documented intended behavior*, not a defect (LANGUAGE_FEATURES.md: "Only direct parameter assignments at `__init__` top level; computed expressions (`self.f = 0`, `self.f = g()`) still require an explicit class-level annotation"), so it is filed here rather than in BUGS.md -- but it deserves revisiting on reachability grounds: `self.count = 0` is one of the most common lines in any Python constructor, the error names the field rather than the rule, and it costs a new user their first ten minutes with no hint that a class-level annotation is the fix. Two independent moves, either or both: (a) **widen the inference** -- a literal RHS (int / float / str / bool / an empty container with an annotated sibling) has an unambiguous type under the existing literal rules, so the auto-declare could cover it without opening general expression inference; the `default_int` interaction and the CPython-parity story are the things to settle, plus whether widening to *any* typed expression is preferable to a literal-only carve-out (a class's field set then depends on arbitrary `__init__` body analysis, which is the reason the rule is narrow today). (b) **fix the diagnostic** -- if the rule stays as is, the error should name the rule and the remedy ("assign a parameter, or declare `count: <type>` at class level") instead of only reporting a missing field; that is cheap and independent of (a). Design decision either way, not a mechanical change -- needs `/tpy-add-feature` if (a) is taken. Surfaced writing a first CPython-interop extension by hand (a plain `self.count = 0` in an `@export class`); reproduces in any class, ext module or not.
- **Relax the nested-type / same-class-member collision rejection using the shadow-qualification mechanism.** A class declaring both a nested type and a same-named field/method is still a hard sema error (`Class 'X' declares both a nested type 'Y' and a field/method 'Y'`, `analyzer.py`) -- distinct from the sibling-type collision (now fixed by fully-qualifying the shadowed type inside the record's emission). The same mechanism (`_qualify_shadowed_nominals` + `local_qualified_cpp_names`, which already registers nested records by qname) could likely qualify `::tpyapp::mod::Outer::Inner` and lift the rejection, matching CPython (which allows it). Extra subtlety: the nested type is declared *inside* the struct, so verify a member declared before it doesn't still shadow the in-struct declaration point. Low value (rare shape, clean diagnostic today). Surfaced fixing the member-name/type-name sibling collision.
- **Optional-typed fields on `@native` records; then upgrade OSError's attrs to close the `None` divergence.** No `@native` record carries an `X | None` field today -- the C++ member would be `std::optional<...>`, `native_field` access codegen would need optional-member handling, and Optional STRING fields hit the borrow-form/storage-form duality for views (the recurring bug-class area). If that capability lands, upgrade `OSError.errno/strerror/filename/filename2` from the `0`/`""` sentinels to true Optionals: the only observable divergences the sentinels leave are `e.errno is None` (currently a loud compile error; falsiness is the documented spelling) and printing the raw unset attribute (`0` vs `None`) -- equality and truthiness already behave CPython-identically (probe-verified: `Optional[int32] == int32` compiles and returns False when empty). Declared in LANGUAGE_FEATURES until then. Surfaced re-examining the sentinel decision on the oserror-exact branch.
- **User-defined `__raise__` on Throwable subclasses (pure-TPy dispatching raises).** Sema currently rejects a user `__raise__` (`error_throwable_user_override_raise`: the Throwable ABI methods are codegen-auto-emitted and an override would collide) -- but the collision is mechanical, not principled: codegen could emit the user's body instead of the auto `throw *this`. Allowing it would let pure-TPy code express the OSError-style ctor-time-decision raise dispatch (`e = MyError(code, msg); raise e` surfacing a subclass) that today needs `@native` interop + `@virtual_raise`; a raising factory function covers only the direct-raise half. Design considerations captured now so they aren't rediscovered: (a+c, one design move) codegen appends an implicit `throw *this;` fallthrough to the emitted override, so a body path that returns normally means "throw myself as-is" -- this satisfies the C++ `[[noreturn]]` contract with no raise-only termination analysis AND gives the non-dispatch fallback a spelling that doesn't recurse (`raise self` would re-enter __raise__; falling off the end doesn't); (b) presence of a user `__raise__` implicitly sets the record's `virtual_raise` flag so the fresh-throw peephole is skipped (the explicit `@virtual_raise` decorator stays for `@native` classes, where the compiler can't see the C++ body -- and is now REJECTED on non-native classes as accepted-then-meaningless, see `error_virtual_raise_non_native`); (d) the body must be effectively readonly (const receiver); (e) `clone`/`what` stay auto-emitted (only `__raise__` opens up). CPython has no `__raise__` at all, so this is TPy-only surface -- no parity contract, but the semantics should be documented in EXCEPTION_DESIGN.md when built. Surfaced by the @virtual_raise design discussion on the oserror-exact branch.
- **Bound-coroutines v1 exclusions** (from the create_task/run de-intrinsic + bound-coroutine-handle feature, zero-alloc concrete representation; each is a follow-up, none is silent): (1) *top-level (module-scope) coroutine binding* -- `c = f()` at module level is rejected at the consumption site ("cannot copy non-copyable type 'Cancellable[...]'": globals are not last-use-movable); usable but the diagnostic should name the coroutine and suggest binding inside a function. (2) *All-paths must-consume* -- the "bound coroutine is never consumed" warning fires only for handles never read after binding; a conditionally-consumed handle (consumed in one branch, dropped in the other) gets no diagnostic, and any NON-cancel read clears it (a `.cancel()` receiver read is carved out and no longer silences it; the `.cancel`-on-coroutine type conflation itself remains BUGS-filed). Upgrade to a flow_facts intersection over true consumption points. (3) *Nested defs* -- `unread_coro_locals` drains at each body end, so a nested def's analysis can clear an enclosing body's pending entries (missed warning, never a false one). (4) *Container/field storage* -- coroutines in `list[...]`/fields stay rejected; `Box[Cancellable[T]]` is the owned-storage spelling (unchanged). (4b) *No elegant "await one of two bound coroutines"* -- the ternary over handles is rejected (borrow) and the if/else form leaves the un-awaited handle warning as unconsumed; CPython allows the alias form freely (the loser gets a GC RuntimeWarning). Loud, but a real expressiveness corner of the move-only model. The working spelling today is a branch-selecting factory `-> Own[Cancellable[T]]` (an author-chosen erasure boundary), which also covers heterogeneous-slot needs (see 6a). (4c) *Temp-receiver auto-materialization* -- `c = Counter(40).bump(5)` is rejected (stable-lvalue rule) but COULD work for the provably-local case by hoisting the rvalue receiver into a frame local (precedent: `_lift_borrowed_rvalue_args` does exactly this for inline awaits' statement-scoped borrows); deliberately not done in v1 because the handle's open-ended borrow makes an invisible compiler temp hide escape hazards -- relax once receiver-escape tracking is real, for handles consumed in the same scope with no escape. (5) *Receiver lifetime across escapes* -- a bound method-coroutine's receiver borrow is registered until consumption, but `create_task(c)` / returning the handle only WARN (the task/caller can outlive the receiver); full tracking is the post-THIR escape-analysis milestone. (6) *Borrowing a handle* -- protocol-annotated alias, bare-`Cancellable[T]` borrow param, and ternary-over-handles are all rejected (handles are consume-only); real borrow support is post-THIR work. (6a) *Erased LOCALS have no explicit spelling* -- the `Own[Cancellable[T]]` local-annotation escape hatch was REMOVED (locals never take Own[] anywhere in TPy); erased locals now arise only from signature boundaries (factory returns / Own params). If a first-class erased-local need appears (heterogeneous slot beyond bind-to-a-new-name), the vocabulary is `Box[Cancellable[T]]` -- construction compiles today, but consuming through the Box (await / create_task via take()) is unwired; design + wire it then. (6b) *Template-frame callees bind erased* -- an async def with static-protocol / `Fn` params has a templated frame whose struct name needs call-site deduction, so its binding falls back to the erased handle (a signature-visible, documented boundary); a zero-alloc form needs deduced-frame naming at bind time. Covered by `async_bind_template_fallback`. (6c) *Cross-module bind* -- the module_qual-qualified concrete-struct naming path is covered by `async_bind_cross_module` (bare-import + from-import forms). (7) *Static coroutine-only check is launderable* -- `create_task`/`run` accept any value whose static type is `Cancellable[T]`, so a conforming non-coroutine record behind a `-> Own[Cancellable[T]]` factory passes and runs where CPython raises TypeError/ValueError; declared divergence (crash-direction under CPython), a full fix needs runtime coroutine branding.
- **Protocol conformance for built-in and generic-container types (incl. conditional conformance).** Bounds + protocols already give monomorphized per-type method dispatch -- `def f[T: P](x: T) -> str: return x.m()` resolves and recurses correctly for USER types (verified). The gap that blocks all type-directed stdlib code is conformance COVERAGE: (1) built-ins already REACH structural conformance (the builtin extends-check is a positive fast-path that falls through, not a short-circuit) and conform fine to protocols whose methods they DECLARE as stub methods (e.g. `__add__` on `int32`); but an intrinsic dunder that exists only as a C++ free function (`tpy::__str__(int32_t)`, `dunder.hpp`), not a declared stub method, is invisible to the structural check -- so `int32` fails a `Stringable {__str__}` bound. Leaves whose required method is C++-only can't participate. (2) No conditional/parametric conformance for generic containers -- no way to state "`list[T]` conforms to `P` when `T` conforms to `P`" (a blanket instance); conformance is per-concrete structural match only. (3) (minor) type-arg inference doesn't fire for a protocol-bounded generic from a built-in arg (needs explicit `[T]`). Fix surface: make built-ins' C++-only intrinsic dunders visible to `sema/protocols.py` structural conformance (declare them as stub methods mapped to the C++ free function, or have conformance consult the intrinsic surface), plus a conditional-conformance concept in the type system. The existing stdlib `Stringable`/`Truthy`/`Representable` protocols are the direct test bed. This is the SHARED prerequisite for two big goals: (a) type-directed serialization in pure stdlib -- zero-copy `json.dumps`/`csv`/`repr` (see the json entry under Next); and (b) **moving `print`/`str` OUT of the compiler** -- they are compiler-blessed today (`gen_print` + the C++ `printing.hpp` printers) precisely because containers/scalars can't conform to a `Display`-style protocol in stdlib. Foundational language feature -- design-doc-worthy `/tpy-add-feature`, not an ad-hoc change. Exploratory design started in `docs/PROTOCOL_CONFORMANCE_DESIGN.md` (keep structural + add nominal impls, singledispatch-shaped; open pivot is method-protocol vs typeclass-function dispatch). Surfaced designing zero-copy json.dumps (the free-function-overload route also dead-ends: `render(e: T)` inside `render[T](list[T])` can't resolve because overloads resolve once with `T` abstract, not per instantiation -- which is why the protocol/bound route, not overloads, is the path).
- **Recognize NumPy scalar types as a CPython-compatible numeric vocabulary.**
  Goal: source using `from numpy import int32` or `import numpy as np` can run
  under CPython with real NumPy and no `tpy` package, while TPy compiles the
  supported scalars to native fixed-width types. Proposed initial surface:
  `int8/16/32/64`, `uint8/16/32/64`, and `float32/64` in annotations and scalar
  constructors, including qualified and aliased imports. Example:
  `def increment(x: np.int32) -> np.int32: return x + np.int32(1)`.
  Assess a compiler-side `numpy` facade using existing library/import/re-export
  machinery; CPython must continue importing real NumPy. Arrays, ufuncs,
  `numpy.typing`, and general NumPy API compilation are separate scope.
  **Design decision before implementation:** native storage widths match, but
  exact aliases to TPy scalar types do not guarantee NumPy semantics. TPy checks
  integer arithmetic overflow; NumPy scalar arithmetic can wrap with a warning.
  Audit mixed-width/signedness and Python-scalar promotion, out-of-range
  construction, division, float precision/formatting, and runtime type checks.
  Choose and document the supported NumPy version range (promotion changed in
  NumPy 2.0). Decide aliases versus distinct semantic types through
  `/tpy-add-feature`; do not silently accept arithmetic with different results
  or choose new warnings/escape hatches without approval. TPy-only members such
  as `int32.add_wrap()` are unavailable on real NumPy types. An annotation such
  as `x: np.int32 = 1` does not convert the value under CPython; explicit
  construction is needed when the runtime scalar type matters.
  **Validation:** run parity cases against real NumPy, covering every proposed
  scalar family, import spelling, annotations/constructors, numeric boundaries,
  mixed operations, and errors/warnings. Decide the test-only NumPy dependency
  and version coverage; keep it separate from the compiler runtime dependency.
  Reuse existing scalar lowering where semantics agree, document the supported
  subset in `LANGUAGE_FEATURES.md` and `TPY_FOR_AGENTS.md`, and consult before
  regenerating changed existing snapshots.
- **Unify ownership and trait annotations through `typing.Annotated` (`Own`/`readonly`/`Send`/`Sync`).**
  Goal: let user source express these contracts under CPython using only the
  stdlib, without importing `tpy`. Make `Annotated[T, "own"]`,
  `Annotated[T, "readonly"]`, `Annotated[T, "send"]`, and
  `Annotated[T, "sync"]` the common annotation mechanism, including combinations
  such as `Annotated[T, "own", "send"]`. Define `type Own[T] = Annotated[T, "own"]`
  in `tpy` as an ordinary convenience alias. Direct annotations, imported aliases,
  and user-defined aliases must have identical compiler meaning, independent of
  the alias's name or defining module. Under CPython these are annotations only;
  ordinary type checkers see the underlying type. Ownership and thread-safety
  enforcement remain TPy's responsibility.
  **Preserve the other roles of existing names.** `readonly` also supports
  `@readonly` and `@readonly(False)`; bare `Send` and `Sync` are protocols used
  in bounds such as `class Sender[T: Send]`. Unify their annotation interpretation
  first, preserving these APIs. Converting those exported names into ordinary
  aliases requires a separate decision about decorator and trait-bound spellings;
  do not silently break them or choose replacement names during implementation.
  **Compiler invariant:** after alias expansion and marker normalization, all
  spellings reach the existing ownership/mutability/trait representations and
  validation. Reuse generic-alias resolution in `parse/type_resolver.py` and
  `_refloat_markers`/`make_send_marker`/`make_sync_marker`; metadata asserts the
  existing Send/Sync contracts, never grants those traits unchecked. Recognize
  `typing.Annotated` through import resolution, ignore unrelated metadata per
  PEP 593, and preserve marker placement through nesting and generic substitution.
  Audit early consumers: constructor field inference currently inspects
  `tpy:Own` before generic aliases expand. Also check bootstrap imports and
  alias re-exports. This is an architectural change requiring `/tpy-add-feature`,
  not a guaranteed parser-only addition or a promise of zero snapshot churn.
  **Compatibility:** the CPython `Own` stub currently allows `Own(value)` and
  `Own[T](value)` as identity calls; a PEP 695 alias does not. Audit callers and
  decide migration explicitly. Annotation introspection also changes. Python
  3.12+ already matches the project's minimum version.
  **Validation:** compare direct/imported/user-alias spellings across parameters,
  returns, constructor field inference, generic and nested types, Optional/union,
  tuples, and generator/async signatures; retain current errors for invalid
  marker positions and failed traits. Cover combined markers, unrelated metadata,
  and unchanged decorator/bound APIs. Use mutation-sensitive or non-copyable
  reference-type cases to detect changed ownership behavior. Update
  `LANGUAGE_FEATURES.md` and `TPY_FOR_AGENTS.md`; consult before regenerating
  changed existing snapshots.
  **Related optional work:** packaging `lib/cpy/tpy` as an installable runtime
  remains useful for other TPy APIs (same wheel vs separate distribution is open).
  Imported metadata sentinels and per-parameter `# tpy: own` comments are separate
  possible extensions, not prerequisites for the string-metadata design.
- Named-constant (value-pattern) field comparison in class patterns: `case Dog(size=Size.BIG):` is rejected across all subject kinds (record, union, polymorphic) with a guard hint, while the literal form `case Dog(size=4):` works. Only *literal* field comparisons are emitted -- `_record_field_conditions` (`tpyc/codegen_cpp/match.py`) handles `TpyLiteralPattern` and union field guards, not `TpyValuePattern`; sema rejects value patterns in `MatchAnalyzer._resolve_class_pattern_fields` (`tpyc/sema/match.py`). Workaround: a guard (`case Dog() if d.size == Size.BIG:`). Fix: lower the value-pattern's dotted-name expression (enum member / module constant) and emit `__case.size == <value>`, mirroring the literal branch -- one site in `_record_field_conditions` plus dropping the sema rejection; benefits record/union/polymorphic uniformly since they share that helper. Also extend the dedup/exhaustiveness key (`MatchAnalyzer._field_constraint_key`) to fold the value constraint, as the literal branch already does. Surfaced finishing literal field-value matching.
- Property narrowing not supported: `if f.val is not None: f.val + 1` does not narrow because property access is a method call (could return different values). Same as function calls. Workaround: `v = f.val; if v is not None: v + 1`. Could support narrowing for simple field-returning getters in the future (requires getter body analysis).
- Tuple iteration + Iterable conformance bundle. `for x in some_tuple:` fails sema with "Cannot iterate over type tuple[...]", and passing a tuple (literal or bound variable) to an `Iterable[T]` param fails conformance in `sema/protocols.py`. Real CPython compat gap -- `math.prod((1.0, 2.0, 3.0))` works in CPython, errors in TPy. Coupled fix needed: (1) sema `type_conforms_to_protocol` case for TupleType when all element types widen to T; (2) codegen emits a std::array-style view from `std::tuple<T, T, ...>` for iteration (std::tuple has no begin/end); (3) for-loop codegen dispatches to that view for tuple iterables. Doing just (1) would make sema accept code that then fails C++ template instantiation (the class of bug we've been cleaning up). Workaround: bind to `list[T]` first or pass a list literal. Surfaced while making math.prod/fsum/sumprod/dist take Iterable[float]; those are now done but skip tuple inputs.
- **Collapse the hand-kept fixed-int name lists onto one source.** `qnames.FIXED_INT_NAMES` (and the `SCALAR_TYPE_NAMES` set built from it), `parse/parser.py:_FIXED_INT_NAMES`, `sema/literal_utils.py:_FIXED_INT_NAMES`, `macro_api.py:_FIXED_INT_NAMES` and `parse/type_resolver.py:_FIXED_INT_MAP` each spell the eight names; `typesys.ALL_FIXED_INTS` is the natural owner and `test_type_def_registry.py`'s drift test covers only three of the copies (not `qnames`). Derive the rest from `ALL_FIXED_INTS`, or extend the drift test to every copy. Surfaced by /tpy-review of the scalar-type rename.
- **A LITERAL at a value union still lands where the C++ converting constructor puts it.** Typed values now land by construction (`_union_member_order`: exact member, then fixed width before BigInt), but an int literal at `uint8 | int` or `float32 | float` renders bare and `std::variant` picks the alternative under its narrowing rule; sema's ranking mirrors that rule so the two agree, and `tests/cases/union/fixed_int_literal_member` pins every shape. Making sema's choice binding would render the literal at the chosen member (`uint8_t{5}`), which today trips the value-union arg and var-decl rows that expect the bare literal (`_union_coerced_literal_arg`); do it when a shape needs a placement the C++ rule refuses.
- **Scalar-type shadow warning: match captures.** `_warn_scalar_type_shadows` sees params, locals, tuple unpack, walrus, for/with targets, nested-def names, comprehension vars, `except ... as` and module-level bindings; a `match` capture named after a scalar type (`case Point(x=int32):`) binds through `sema/match.py` and is not recorded, so it does not warn. Extend when the match binding path grows a declaration hook. Also accepted for now: the gate requires the binding to be imported straight from `tpy`, so a scalar re-exported through a user module (`from mymod import int32`) is not recognized.
- **tpy-lang.org still spells the scalar types CapWords.** The site lives in its own repo; apply the same word-bounded rename (`Int8..UInt64`, `Float32`, `Float64`, `Char` -> lowercase) there so examples match the compiler.
- No `AnyInt` protocol covering BigInt + all `AnyFixedInt`. `AnyFixedInt` bounds a generic to fixed-width ints only (excludes BigInt). Writing a generic stdlib function like `gcd[T: AnyInt](a: T, b: T) -> T` that accepts BigInt *and* any fixed-width int has no natural bound. Surfaces when trying to write pure-TPy generics over int types (`math.gcd`, `math.isqrt`, anywhere int-algebraic). Workaround: declare as `int`-only (forces BigInt; small-int callers pay widening cost). Fix: add an `AnyInt` protocol in `lib/tpy/tpy/_core/_types.py` that unions BigInt + AnyFixedInt, with the arithmetic/comparison surface needed for common algorithms.
- Generic type params over int types can't use basic arithmetic without a bound. Pure-TPy `def gcd[T](a: T, b: T) -> T` rejects `a = -a` ("Cannot reassign parameter"; workaround: copy to local), `x = -x` on T ("Invalid operand type for unary '-'"), and `abs(x)` on T ("No matching overload for abs(T)"). Each is because T has no known signed-int bound. Resolving via the `AnyInt` protocol above (with `__neg__` / `__abs__` surface) would unblock pure-TPy integer generics. An explicit `[T: AnyFixedInt]` bound does not help either: `def twice[T: AnyFixedInt](v: T) -> T: return v + v` rejects with `Invalid operand types for '+': Ref[T] and Ref[T]`, because `AnyFixedInt` is a bodyless `@native` marker protocol (a C++ concept) with no operator surface sema can consult (surfaced 2026-09-12 while writing `int/scalar_type_names`, whose bounded section is an identity function for that reason). The ban on reassigning generic-typed parameters is probably separate and may warrant its own review -- for some patterns it's a real ergonomic tax.
- No `Numeric` (or `AnyNumber`) protocol covering `AnyInt + float + float32`. Blocks writing a generic `math.prod[T: Numeric](Iterable[T], *, start: T = 1) -> T` and similar generic numerics. `start: T = 1` works at sema (int literal coerces to T via normal default-value coercion; verified), so the only missing piece is the bound itself plus its declared arithmetic surface (`__mul__`, `__add__` at minimum). Depends on `AnyInt` above. Once both land, `prod` can be a single generic instead of N overloads, avoiding the empty-list W2 ambiguity entirely. Broader payoff: unblocks user-written generic numeric code (vector math, statistics fragments, aggregation primitives) that currently has no bound to use.
- No trivially-relocatable / primitive-value trait: value types that can be memcpy'd (fixed ints, bool, char, floats, plain aggregates of those) vs value types with owning buffers (`BigInt`, `str`, `bytes`). A `TriviallyRelocatable[T]`-style marker (name open: trivial? primitive?) would let generic containers/algorithms pick memcpy/realloc fast paths and bound `@noalloc`-friendly APIs. Needs `/tpy-add-feature` (trait vocabulary + auto-derivation, like Send/Sync). Scoped for 0.6.0 (RELEASE_PLAN).
- Atomic shared-ownership smart pointer in TPy: `Arc[T]` (atomic refcounts). Non-atomic `Rc[T]` and its `Weak[T]` companion ship in `tplib` for single-threaded use; the multi-threaded analog is a v3+ item (multi-threaded executor, multi-awaiter Future). Open design: refcount-update memory ordering (acquire/release vs seq-cst on each refcount op), `Weak[T]`'s atomic upgrade compare-exchange shape, and interaction with cross-thread async primitives + a `Sync` bound on T.
- `thread_local` storage in TPy. v1.2 step 7 collapsed the C++-side `executor_ops` global entirely; the only remaining shared async state is `_current_executor: Ptr[Executor]` in `lib/tpy/asyncio/_executor.py`, also a plain (single-process) global. The TLS upgrade is gated on multi-threaded async (v3+) actually landing; until then `thread_local` is purely a future-proofing item, not a porting blocker.
- TPy method bodies on `@native` classes. Today the compiler enforces "methods on @native classes must have '...' body" (`tpyc/sema/analyzer.py:1624`). Constructors via `@overload @cpp_template` work, but instance methods are stub-only. v1.2 step 7 deleted both `Waker` and `ExecutorHandle` from C++ (Waker is now pure TPy, ExecutorHandle is gone), so the original async-side motivation is moot. The gap is still real for other `@native` types that might want TPy method bodies (none on the immediate roadmap). Open question for the design: how the TPy body resolves field access on a C++-owned struct, and whether to allow mixing stub methods + body methods on the same class.
- `imported_protocol_qualification` (`tpyc/typesys.py`) consults `ProtocolInfo.module` (the public re-export module), while the record-side analog uses `RecordInfo.defining_module` (the actual private submodule). If a `@dynamic` protocol ever lives in a private submodule re-exported under a different public name (the `tpy._builtins._bytes` -> `tpy` pattern records use), `qualified_cpp_name` would emit the wrong namespace for cross-module refs. Currently safe because no `@dynamic` protocol uses that re-export pattern; add `defining_module` to `ProtocolInfo` if/when one does. Surfaced by /tpy-review of v1.2 step 7.
- `self.x: T = value` field declarations in `__init__` (audit B127). The single most common Python field-declaration idiom is rejected with an opaque "Invalid assignment target" (the parser refuses any annotated non-Name target); TPy forces the class-level-annotation + bare-assign split. Design approved in outline: accept in `__init__` only -- the annotation declares the field (equivalent to the class-level annotation) or validates against an existing one; conflicting types error; outside `__init__` stays rejected with a message pointing at both spellings. Needs `/tpy-add-feature` (field-registration interplay, MIL-init ordering). All four shapes rejected today: scalar + container, with and without the class-level annotation. Split out of the parser-fidelity cluster fix per approval.
- `NoReturn` return-type support. The missing-return check (a non-None return type must terminate on every path) cannot see that a trailing call never returns -- `def f() -> int32: ...; sys.exit(1)` is rejected even though the call cannot fall through, because TPy has no `NoReturn` type to declare on `sys.exit` / panic wrappers (`lib/tpy/sys.py` carries the matching TODO). Workaround: end with `raise` or an `assert False`. Fix shape: accept `NoReturn` as a return annotation, treat a call to a `NoReturn` function as a terminator in `liveness.stmts_terminate`, and declare it on `sys.exit` and the raise-wrapper stubs. Surfaced implementing the missing-return check.
- Match guard lowering still has three open-coded copies of the shape the shared helpers capture: `_emit_optional_inner_record` / `_emit_optional_inner_if_elif` fold guards into the arm condition instead of routing through `_gen_match_optional_cond` + `_emit_guarded_arm_tail` (safe today only because `_partition_optional_cases` bails guard+binding arms to the fixed chain), and `_gen_match_polymorphic_guarded` open-codes the guard-tail (guard-if + goto + close). Unify all three onto the helpers so the next pattern kind can't reintroduce the severed-chain/binding-after-guard bug class; while there, replace the lone `getattr(case.pattern, "binds_full_optional", False)` read with typed access. All in `tpyc/codegen_cpp/match.py`. Surfaced by /tpy-review of the match-lowering cluster fix.
- `collect_type_args_of_bounded_records` (`tpyc/codegen_cpp/protocols.py:740`) still has an `info.builtin_type_key is None` guard that its sibling `collect_record_types_from_type` dropped in v1.2 step 7. The two helpers now treat in-module `@builtin_type` records inconsistently: if `Waker` (or any other `@builtin_type` record) ever appears as a type arg to a bounded record, the second helper would silently exclude it. Align the two to the same policy. Surfaced by /tpy-review of v1.2 step 7.
- Generic class specializations -- closed by v1.2 step 5 (Poll[T] port). The premise that `Poll[T]` needed a TPy-level specialization mechanism turned out to be wrong: a single `@nocopy class Poll[T]` body with `UninitArrayStorage[T, 1] + bool` storage covers the value-T / void / reference-T / move-only / non-default-constructible cases by composition of existing primitives. The void analog rides on `Poll[None]` -> `Poll<std::monostate>` lowering, the reference-T specialization (`Poll<T&>` in the old C++) was never instantiated by generated code, and `UninitArrayStorage`'s placement-new contract handles move-only / non-default-constructible T identically to `std::optional<T>`. Specialization syntax may still be useful for a future feature, but it's not blocking anything in the async pipeline; left as a research item rather than a tracked TODO.
- `@cpp_template` literal-brace escape syntax. The substitution engine treats `{...}` as a placeholder field name, so C++ aggregate-init / lambda / scope braces in the template string can't be expressed (e.g. `@cpp_template("::tpy::Handle{static_cast<void*>(&{0})}")` fails with `Internal error: unexpected '{' in field name`). Workaround today: wrap the brace-using expression in a templated C++ helper and bind to that helper via `@cpp_template`. Fix: add `{{` / `}}` Python-f-string-style escape syntax. Pairs with the BUGS.md entry on the same code path (UX: produce a clear diagnostic instead of an internal error when literal braces appear). Surfaced during async v1.1 Phase 2.2.
- `Final[list[T]]` / `Final[Array[T, N]]` for compile-time constant tables. Today `Final[T]` only allows primitives (`int`, `float`, `bool`, `str`/`StrView`, `char`, `IntN`) and `tuple` (see `docs/LANGUAGE_FEATURES.md:5071`); array-shaped round-constant tables (SHA-2 H0/K, AES S-boxes, CRC tables, etc.) have no natural spelling. `Final[tuple[uint32, uint32, ..., uint32]]` works but is unwieldy at N=64+ and doesn't compose with `Span[uint32]` consumers without a conversion. A module-level `list[uint32]` heap-allocates once at module init; correct but wrong shape for what is conceptually a `constexpr std::array`. Right surface is probably `Final[Array[uint32, 8]]` -> `inline constexpr std::array<uint32_t, 8>` (header-emitted, no init order, fully constant-folded). Open: whether to also accept `Final[list[T]]` as syntactic sugar that codegens to the same `std::array` (size from initializer length).
- `Stringable` structural protocol + binop acceptance. Any type with `__str__ -> StrView` would conform; `__add__` / `__eq__` / etc. on string-like types (`str`, `String`, `StrView`, plus user types like the Pascal POC's `PStr[N]`) could declare `other: Stringable` once instead of duplicating overloads per concrete operand type. Today the convention is explicit overloads -- see `str.__add__` in `lib/tpy/tpy/_builtins/_types.py:453-464` for the four-way overload set (`str`/`String`/`StrView`/`char`) -- and a user record like `PStr` must repeat the pattern or force translator-side `str(...)` wrapping at call sites (Pascal POC takes the latter route in `frontends/pascal/pascal_translator/translate.py::_coerce_string_operand`). Open design: (a) structural protocol definition with the `__str__ -> StrView` requirement; (b) whether sema's binop-dispatch / argument-coercion path should auto-`__str__` an operand when the formal type is `Stringable` (consistent with how protocols are normally satisfied -- *not* a special-cased implicit coercion); (c) interaction with `char`, which has a string-conversion via `tpy::char_to_str` rather than `__str__`. Non-issue today but cleans up several stdlib overload duplications + lets out-of-tree user string types (PStr / FixStr / future Pascal char-string / future C-string wrappers) state their operand surface once.
- `Out[T]` annotation for by-ref out-parameters (upstream #20). C/C++ APIs commonly return multiple values via by-reference out-params (`void f(Key k, FooBuf*& outFoo, BarBuf*& outBar)`). Porting these to TPy today requires changing the signature shape -- typically a `tuple[Ptr[T], Ptr[T]]` return -- which deviates from source parity. Surface: `def f(k: Key, out_foo: Out[Ptr[FooBuf]], out_bar: Out[Ptr[BarBuf]]) -> None`, lowering to `void f(Key k, FooBuf*& out_foo, BarBuf*& out_bar)`. Two call-site shapes to consider: (a) implicit pack -- `foo, bar = f(k)` and the compiler synthesizes locals bound by reference to the out positions; (b) explicit -- caller declares locals first and passes by name (`f(k, out_foo=foo, out_bar=bar)`). Body-side semantics in both cases: assignments to `Out[T]` parameters write through to the caller's locals. Why it matters: a common codegen shape for helpers that produce more than one value -- with `Out[T]` the port can stay 1:1 with the C++ source. Existing parity gap (recap): tpy already special-cases container parameters to be passed as `T&` / `const T&` based on mutation analysis; `Out[T]` extends that to a user-facing annotation for the case where the caller explicitly wants by-ref semantics regardless of mutation.
- Focused regression test: `@cpp_template` free function taking `Own[T]` of a `@nocopy` type, called with a local at its last use. Should pin the auto-move emission (snapshot shows `std::move(local)` in the expansion). Currently verified only transitively via async tests; a focused test would make the contract explicit and catch regressions cleanly. See v1.2 step 2 in `docs/ASYNC_PROGRESS.md`.
- Regression test for the BUGS "borrow protocol passed to consuming-only sink" entry: an `error_awaitable_non_own_consuming/` case with `# tpyc: error(/...)` would lock in the failure mode and become a regression target when the sema-diagnostic fix lands.
- Regression test for `await asyncio.create_task(sub())` in **discard-result** position (no `result =` binding). The existing `tests/cases/async/await_task_rvalue/` case covers the bind-result form of the ERASED-mode rvalue path; the discard form takes a different codegen branch (no var assignment, just `.reset()` and state transition). Low-priority pin since the underlying mechanism is shared with bind-result, but the codegen paths diverge enough that an explicit test would catch any future drift between them.
- Regression test for `await failed_task` where the task raised a non-`CancelledError` exception. Documents the current slicing behavior (`BaseException` is re-raised, not the concrete subclass) and would catch any future TaskState-exception fix that preserves the dynamic type. Tied to the BUGS entry on "Caught BaseException as e stored into a field slices the dynamic type" -- the test pins the surface symptom.
- Coverage gap: borrow-tracker tests (`tests/cases/pointers/warn_borrow_ptr/`, `tests/cases/pointers/warn_borrow_field_path/`) only exercise the explicit `take_ptr(x)` path. The direct value-to-`Ptr[T]` coercion path (`p: Ptr[T] = x`) now registers the same `PTR` borrow + non-null provenance via the `coerce_expr` mutation hook in `sema/compatibility.py` and the `expr_yields_non_null_ptr` helper in `sema/context.py`, but those wirings have no dedicated regression test. Add `warn_borrow_direct_coercion/` mirroring the take_ptr shape with `p: Ptr[Point] = point` initializers and a rebind line (`p = other_point`) -- the rebind path consumes the same helper but lives at a separate site so a single-site refactor that drops one call can't silently shrink borrow coverage. Surfaced by `/tpy-review` of the value-to-Ptr coercion cleanup.
- Silent-warning gap in `tests/cases/tuple/tuple_optional_ptr_mixed/`. After the value-to-Ptr coercion now fires the mutation signal, the case emits a new "Mutation while borrowed" warning in `diag.txt` but the `main.py` source has no `# tpyc: warning(/.../)` annotation pinning it. Snapshots will keep passing because the diagnostic is captured, but the annotation-validator can't confirm the warning is intentional and a future regression that silently drops the warning would only fail at snapshot-diff level, not at the annotation level. Add the `# tpyc: warning(...)` marker on the offending line so the test's intent is explicit. Surfaced by `/tpy-review` of the value-to-Ptr coercion cleanup.
- Coverage expansion for pointer-form generator/coro frame slots (post `fix-coro-frame-optional-nonvalue`). Four missing variants: (a) standalone state-machine sync generator over `list[NonValue]` with multi-yield body to isolate the pointer-form loop var from the tuple-yield shape in `tests/cases/tuple/tuple_optional_yield_prev/`; (b) async coroutine with a `for x in list[NonValue]: await ...` body (non-Optional element) -- exercises the CFG-decomposed for-loop frame path; (c) generator-method variant on a class with `def gen(self) -> Iterator[...]` returning pointer-form data -- covers the `record_name != None` branch of `_gen_generator_code`; (d) async coroutine method with `Optional[NonValue]` local across an await -- covers the `record_name != None` branch of `_gen_coro_code`. Surfaced by `/tpy-review` of the coro-frame-optional-nonvalue fix.
- Pre-existing TpyCall non-null predicate duplicated at two sites that the `expr_yields_non_null_ptr` consolidation didn't fold in: `tpyc/sema/statements.py:2925-2941` (borrow-registration site -- repeats the `init.call_type.is_pointer() or fi.value_ptr_coercion` test plus a hardcoded coercion-name list that's now redundant with `Coercion.produces_non_null_ptr`) and `tpyc/sema/compatibility.py:1693-1697` (dangling-return classification -- same TpyCall predicate). Fold both into the helper (or a sibling that returns the discriminating call info) so a future change to "what counts as a Ptr-yielding call" lives in one place. Out of scope for the original refactor; surfaced by `/simplify` review of the value-to-Ptr coercion cleanup.
- Coverage gap: `Diagnostic.format` in `tpyc/diagnostics.py` now prefers `loc.file` over the caller-supplied fallback name (so a frontend plugin's diagnostics point into the DSL source, not the generated `.py`), but no test exercises the `loc.file`-set path. Add a `tpyc/`-level unit test on `Diagnostic.format` with a location carrying its own file (toolchain-free), or a frontend-plugin error case that surfaces a `.pas`-file location. Surfaced by `/tpy-review` of the enum-field-default branch.
- Coverage gap: enum-member field default honoring a `@native` member rename. `_render_enum_member_default` (`tpyc/codegen_cpp/records.py`) maps the member through `einfo.cpp_member_name_map`, but the happy-path test only uses pure-Python enums whose member names pass through unchanged. Add a case with a `@native` enum whose member has a C++-name override used as a field default, to pin the rename emission. Surfaced by `/tpy-review` of the enum-field-default branch.
- Coverage gap: cross-module *bad* enum member as a field default. The happy path covers cross-module enum defaults and the error path covers a same-module bad member, but no case names a non-existent member of an *imported* enum (`state: RemoteState = RemoteState.NONEXISTENT`). Add an error case to pin the registration-time rejection when the enum is cross-module. Surfaced by `/tpy-review` of the enum-field-default branch.
- **CPython-shape heterogeneous variadic-tuple `gather`**. v1.5 M9 ships two homogeneous entrypoints -- `asyncio.gather(*tasks: Task[T]) -> list[T]` (variadic-positional) and `asyncio.gather_list(tasks: list[Task[T]]) -> list[T]` (list shape) -- both requiring all tasks to share return type `T`. The CPython-shape *heterogeneous* form `gather[*Ts](*coros: Awaitable[*Ts]) -> tuple[*Ts]` requires variadic generics (TPy doesn't have them) plus the async-def `*args` codegen fix in BUGS.md. When both prerequisites land, the heterogeneous form coexists with the homogeneous shapes as an overload of `gather` (distinguished by element-type uniformity). Until then, mixed-type concurrent fetches use the `create_task` + `await task` pattern.
- **Builtin functions: the remaining gaps after the 2026-10-02 batch.** (1) `max(xs, default=v)` / `min(xs, default=v)`: no overload (an empty iterable raises `ValueError`). (2) `next(it, None)`: the default has the element's type; a `T | None` result of a reference `T` is the storage-form Optional (a copy), so it waits for the Optional-return design (`builtins/error_next_default_none`). (3) `max` / `min` over an iterable and `next(it, default)` return a class instance (or a list, a dict, ...) as the element itself where a container lends it (never through an iterator: a warned copy there), since 2026-10-02; tuples holding one are refused, and the one-argument `next(it)` over class instances still is (the entry below, "A native generic's `-> T` result ... binds as a borrow"); `sorted()` still copies them silently, a separate fix (`BUGS.md#sorted-ref-element-copy-unwarned`). (4) Two-argument `max("a", "b")` / `max((1, 2), (1, 3))`: the scalar overloads cover fixed ints, `int` and `float` only (*does not satisfy 'AnyFixedInt'*), while the one-iterable form takes any comparable value type. (5) Hygiene: `_star_elem_print_form` (tpyc/thir/lower/checks.py) is a second type-to-`PrintForm` classifier beside `_print_arg_form` -- one type-keyed classifier should serve both; a member-less protocol's C++ concept (`ComparableValue`) renders only its inherited methods, not the conjunction of its parents' concepts (sema enforces the bound, so harmless today).
- **[design] Iterator provenance: an iterator's steps either outlive the iterator or do not, and the type carries which (SCHEDULED third after the borrow-result merge: method borrows, builtin keyword arguments, then this; user, 2026-10-04, 'a tough topic').** Today an `Iterator[T]` over a reference `T` means 'a reference valid until the next step', a lifetime no type carries, so `max` / `min` / `next(it, d)` over ANY iterator copy the element with a warning, and two `next` steps in one expression are refused by a stopgap (`BUGS.md#next-step-reference-outlived-by-advance`). CPython keeps the object alive by refcount; Rust has two kinds of iterator and forbids the third: `Item = &'a T` lends with the SOURCE's lifetime, `Item = T` hands out owned values, and a reference into a frame local cannot escape the step. The unit gives TPy those two kinds: (1) a LENDING verdict per iterator type -- for a view a stub hands out (`iter(ps)`, `reversed(ps)`, `d.values()`) a declared fact 'steps point into the viewed container' on the iterator type (beside `borrowing_view=` / `elements=` in the `@native` keyword grammar, docs/NATIVE_INTEROP.md); for a GENERATOR a sema-derived verdict 'every yield is rooted in storage the frame borrows (its reference arguments), none in a frame local', read off the per-yield roots the yield-dangle check already classifies (`pending_yield_root_checks`, `generic_yield_borrows`, `tpyc/sema/statements.py`) and recorded on the generator's FunctionInfo beside `return_borrows_from` (which records frame CAPTURES, not step origins -- the two are different facts); a user iterator class lends when its `__next__` returns a borrow rooted in a field the class itself borrows. `iter_element_source` (`tpyc/sema/iter_loans.py`) then answers HANDLE-lends vs HANDLE-copies from the fact, and the `for` statement's loop variable gets the same verdict (today `best = p` out of a generator loop is refused for every generator). (2) OWNING iterators: `Iterator[Own[T]]` as a `max` / `min` / `next` source MOVES the winner out (`-> Own[T]`, no copy, CPython-identical since the object is unique); today refused (`builtins/error_min_max_own_iterator`). When both land: the copy warning stays only for a generator that yields a frame local it rebinds (the one shape Rust refuses outright -- decide then whether TPy keeps the warned copy or refuses it too), `next(g, d)` over a lending generator is a BORROW of the source and the two-steps stopgap retires. Hard parts to size first: the generator verdict is a whole-body fact settled after body analysis (the `_settle_deferred_generic_yields` precedent), a yield rooted in a captured CONTAINER's element lends while one rooted in a captured scalar's field may not, and the runtime helpers need a third entry beside lend / copy (move) -- probe the corpus for how many generators are lending before designing the verdict. Related: `BUGS.md#iter-local-over-literal-dangles`, `comp-iter-rvalue-source`, the borrow-result entry below.
- **[design] A native generic's `-> T` result that IS one of its arguments' elements binds as a borrow, not a copy -- what remains (2026-10-02).** `borrows=(...)` / `element_of=(...)` (keywords of `@native` / `@cpp_template`) (docs/NATIVE_INTEROP.md) covers `min` / `max` with two or three operands, over one iterable (with and without `key=`) and `next(it, default)`: the result is a borrow wherever every named argument lends storage that outlives the call (an lvalue; for an `element_of=` parameter, a container -- `iter_element_source` in `tpyc/sema/iter_loans.py`, the classification the for statement uses), a value otherwise, and a binding or owning slot that holds such a value warns. An ITERATOR never lends, its step being valid only until the next one. Still open: (1) aliasing through an iterator that only VIEWS storage outliving the call -- a named `it = iter(ps)`, an inline `reversed(ps)` -- is a warned copy; letting it borrow needs a declared "steps point into the viewed container" fact on the iterator type, which no iterator stub states today (a dict's `values()` view and a record whose `__iter__` hands out a borrowing view, such as `ArrayList`, lend since 2026-10-02: `IterElementSource.CONTAINER`); (2) sources yielding `Own[T]` (`Iterator[Own[T]]`) hand out fresh elements, so no borrow is possible and the result should be a silent value -- today the form is refused (`builtins/error_min_max_own_iterator`); (3) the one-argument `q = next(it)` over class instances is refused at lowering (`expr.call:call.error_return`); (4) tuples holding a class instance are refused at every form: the native stub result is refused until the borrow-form tuple result exists (`BUGS.md#min-max-key-result-copies`) -- the same gap as an element of such a list returned by a concrete function (`BUGS.md#tuple-elem-return-borrow-form-rejects`) or its generic twin (`BUGS.md#generic-tuple-elem-return-ill-formed`); (5) the decorator on a METHOD is rejected (the method call path does not take the call-site stamp; "Callable-level borrow annotation for native stubs: the remaining users" above); (6) PRECISE const: a call whose result is a mutable reference is a mutable use of every operand that lends it (`CallAnalyzer._mark_borrow_result_operands_written`), as a generic returning its parameter is, so `m = min(a, b, key=f); return m.v` takes `P& a, P& b`; keeping the operands const until something writes through the result is a whole-function question, not per-writer patches; (7) a copy the call hands back (over an iterator) at a WRITTEN parameter of a method or constructor is refused (`method.arg_shape`): only the free-call family hoists it into a temporary, which then warns; (8) the GENERIC-BODY policy (decided 2026-10-02: conservative): in a generic body over a protocol-typed source (`def top[T](xs: Iterable[T]): m = max(xs)`) the verdict is decided before instantiation -- a hedged copy (`may copy T into local 'm' if not a value type`, the generic copy contract) and the lost-write error; the widening is "Per-instantiation result form for a generic body" below, and a `list[T]` source cannot hold its borrow yet (`BUGS.md#generic-container-borrow-result-unusable`); (9) aug-assign through `min` / `max` / `next` is refused until aug-assign binds its receiver once ("Aug-assign binds its receiver / index once" below); (10) `copy(...)` is exempted from the deferred argument-copy warning by its qualified name (`CallAnalyzer.defer_argument_copies`); declaring `def copy[T](x: readonly[T]) -> Own[T]` would let the readonly-parameter rule cover it; (12) RETIRE the stopgap that refuses two advances of one iterator in one expression (`iterator_advanced_twice`, `BUGS.md#next-step-reference-outlived-by-advance`) once MIR models the step loan; (11) hygiene: `_declares_element_cursor` (`tpyc/sema/iter_loans.py`) maps a pending literal to its container beside `_as_container` (`tpyc/sema/type_join.py`) -- one mapping; and "is the callee emitted const" is spelled twice in `tpyc/sema/calls.py` (`resolve_pending_readonly_receiver_checks`, `resolve_pending_copy_receiver_calls`) -- one `FunctionInfo` property. NOT part of it: `sorted()` copying class instances (`BUGS.md#sorted-ref-element-copy-unwarned`) -- it returns a new owned list, so its fix is the element-copy warning gate (`Iterable[Own[T]]`), blocked on `BUGS.md#sorted-of-iter-call`.
- **[thir] Aug-assign binds its receiver / index once.** `target OP= value` lowers the target twice (`_lower_stmt` aug-assign arm, `tpyc/thir/lower/statements.py`), so a call on the receiver chain or in an index runs twice where CPython runs it once: a user borrow-returning call (`pick(b).v += 5`), a side-effecting `@auto_readonly` getter (a Mutex guard's `g.get().n += 1` is pure, but a counting getter is not), a property and a user `__getitem__` (held at a reject), `min` / `max` / `next` (refused in sema). Bind the receiver and every index once through the shared THIR receiver-splitting machinery -- the class-constant leg's `recv_eval` / `recv_wrap` split is the precedent -- which closes `BUGS.md#augassign-call-receiver-double-eval` for every callee and lifts those refusals. The side-effect COUNT does not wait for the evaluation-order policy. Filed 2026-10-02.
- **[design] Per-instantiation result form for a generic body.** `max` / `min` / `next` (and every declared-borrow stub) over a protocol-typed source take the form of the INSTANTIATION, so the generic equals its twin -- lifts the hedged copy at `Iterable[T]` sources (docs/LANGUAGE_FEATURES.md, "the copy contract of a generic body"). Needs sema to re-check the write / sink verdicts per instantiation (monomorphized checking), the same gap behind the generic owning-slot copy contract; the C++ half exists (the runtime already selects lend / copy per instantiation, and asserts only that a `lend` verdict is a lending source). A -> B is a pure widening: every program accepted today stays accepted, only the warned sites start aliasing. Also closes `BUGS.md#generic-container-borrow-result-unusable`. Requested by the user 2026-10-02.
- **[design] Builtin functions take keyword arguments as any function does -- its own unit (decided 2026-10-02: "builtins should work same as normal functions"; built twice inside the builtin-gaps batch and backed out after two review rounds each found a keyword bound to the wrong parameter).** Today a builtin function takes no keyword (`sum(xs, start=5)`, `enumerate(xs, start=1)`, `round(x, ndigits=2)`, `open(p, mode="r")`: *Keyword arguments not supported for builtin ...*) except through `_flatten_key_kwarg` (tpyc/sema/calls.py), which is keyed on the names `sorted` / `min` / `max` and appends `key` (and `sorted`'s `reverse`) positionally before resolution; it is sound only because those stubs are positional-capable, which is also why `sorted(xs, True)` compiles (`BUGS.md#key-arg-accepted-positionally`). Three resolver facts the unit has to design for, each found by breaking it: (a) the builtin overload path (`_analyze_builtin_function_overloads`) finalises the arguments itself and never retypes a keyword argument against the matched parameter, where the user path re-analyses through `_analyze_single_function_call` -- so a lambda passed by keyword matches (Regime C) but its body is never typed; (b) `infer_type_params_for_function` (tpyc/sema/type_ops.py) skips keyword-only parameters, so a type parameter that only a keyword-only parameter names (`K` in `key: Fn[[T], K]`) stays unbound -- user functions have the same gap (`def f[T, K](xs, *, key: Fn[[T], K])`: *Cannot infer type arguments*); (c) a call node is analysed more than once (an argument of a generic, `@dispatch` or method call), and nothing records the keyword binding on it, so any in-place rewrite must give the same answer on a re-analysis -- a rewrite that restricted the candidates or relied on keyword-only marks did not (`first(mod.f(1, key=5), 0)` bound `5` to another overload's parameter; `ident(max(xs, key=lambda v: -v))` was refused). Design direction from the reviews: ONE binder for builtin and user overloads -- resolve with the keywords, place them per the matched overload, record the binding on the call node, retype every argument against the matched parameters -- with inference over keyword-only parameters; then mark the stubs' keyword-only (`*`) and positional-only (`/`) parameters as CPython has them (`sorted(iterable=xs)`, `len(x=xs)` are `TypeError` there), and add the missing keywords (`zip(strict=)`, `pow(mod=)`, `open(encoding=)`) and the type constructors' (`int(x, base=16)`). The stub parameter names already follow CPython (`round(number, ndigits)`, `pow(base, exp)`, `open(file, mode)`). Keyword arguments are evaluated in parameter order by the user path today (`BUGS.md#subexpression-right-to-left-eval`); the builtin path must not be worse. Probes with the failing shapes: `/tmp/agents/bg/review/probes/arch/kw1`..`kw5`, `/tmp/agents/bg/review/probes2/arch/re3`..`re6`, `po`, `pob`, `uk`, `gx`.
- **[design] `print(*x)` admits its source by a fact, not by a type list (user, 2026-10-02: "shouldn't it be generic?"; agreed as a follow-up unit).** `print(*xs)` takes a list, `Array`, `Span` or `*args` pack because `star_source_element_type` (tpyc/sema/expressions.py) tests exactly those four -- the cover-set a user `*args` unpack needs, where the pack IS a `Span`. For `print` the runtime (`::tpy::PrintEach`) walks any range by reference, so a tuple, a set, a dict, `range(3)`, a `str`, `bytes` and a `bytearray` are refused for no reason (*print() can unpack only a list, Array or Span with '*'; got 'set[int32]' ...*). Decided direction: admit any source that is a container the runtime iterates in place -- a `NativeIterable[T]` conformer that is not an iterator -- read off the type's facts; expand a tuple at compile time into its elements (`print(*t)` is `print(t[0], t[1], t[2])`, its elements having different types); keep LAZY sources (a generator, a generator expression, a file) refused with the `print(*list(...))` hint, since CPython finishes unpacking before it prints and a source that prints or raises midway would behave differently, and an implicit materialization is a hidden allocation. Not `Spannable[T]`: that is the right criterion for `*args`, and would exclude set, dict and `range` here. Cases: one section per source kind in `builtins/print_star` with CPython parity; `error_print_star_generator` stays. Related: `Optional` elements and a narrowed source name are refused at lowering (`print.star_elem.optional`, `print.star_narrowed_source`).
- **Star-unpack into varargs: container cover-set is list/span/array only.** `*xs` into a vararg pack (`_unpack_star_element_type` in `tpyc/sema/expressions.py`, and the parallel validation in `_analyze_and_pack_varargs`) accepts only directly-iterable lvalue containers: `list`, `Span`, `Array`, `PendingListType`. CPython permits unpacking any iterable -- `tuple`, `set`, `bytes`, `str`, generators, dict views. This gap is language-wide (affects non-generic varargs too: `sum_all(*tuple)` rejects identically), not specific to the generic path. Expanding it means deciding which iterables codegen can lower into `tpy::varargs<T>` and threading the element-type extraction + the `as_mut_span`-equivalent for each. Separate feature, not a defect. Surfaced during `fix-star-unpack-generic-vararg`.
- **Star-unpack into variadic builtins other than `print` is rejected, not spread.** `print(*xs)` spreads a list / Array / Span / `*args` source (`tests/cases/builtins/print_star`); any other builtin (`max(*xs)`, `min(*xs)`, `len(*xs)`) still does not spread `*unpack`: the unpack is typed as ONE element argument (*No matching overload for max(int32)*, `BUGS.md#own-in-star-unpack-diag`) or stopped by the `analyze_expr` safety net ("the call target does not accept *args"). `print(*opts)` over `Optional` elements is refused at lowering (`print.star_elem.optional`), as is a narrowed source name. User-defined variadic functions/methods support `*list` unpack (the `fix-star-unpack-generic-vararg` work); the remaining builtin handlers don't route their arg analysis through the vararg-pack machinery. Supporting it means teaching each variadic builtin's handler to accept/lower a star-unpack (or routing builtins through the shared vararg packer). Feature, not a defect -- the current behavior is a clean reject. Surfaced during `fix-star-unpack-generic-vararg`.
- **[feature] Mixed positional + star-unpack in one vararg call (`f(a, *xs, b)`, `f(*a, *b)`).** CPython accepts arbitrary interleaving of positionals and unpacks in a call (PEP 448): `sum_all(1, *mid, 2)` -> `sum_all(1, 10, 20, 2)`; `f(*a, *b)` concatenates. TPy currently requires a `*xs` unpack to be the *sole* entry in the vararg region and rejects the mix at sema with "Cannot mix *unpacking with other arguments" (`_analyze_and_pack_varargs` in `tpyc/sema/calls.py`; regression test `tests/cases/calls/error_star_unpack_mixed/`). The reject replaced a *silent miscompile* (codegen's `_gen_vararg_pack` at `tpyc/codegen_cpp/expressions.py:5308` `return`s on the first `TpyStarUnpack`, dropping sibling args -- `sum_all(1, *mid, 2)` gave 30 not 33). This is a divergence from CPython, not a hard limit; the reject is the correct interim.

  **Why it's not a quick patch:** `_gen_vararg_pack` has only two shapes today -- a fixed `std::array<T*, N>`/`std::array<T, N>` for individual args (compile-time N), and a direct `varargs<T>(as_mut_span(xs))` for a lone unpack. A mix has a **runtime** length (the unpack's size is dynamic), so neither shape fits. Supporting it needs:
  1. **Runtime** (`runtime/cpp/include/tpy/varargs.hpp`): a `varargs<T>` constructor over a runtime-sized pointer buffer (it is already dual-mode with an `indirect_` `T* const*`; add a dynamic-size entry, e.g. from `std::span<T* const>` / `const std::vector<T*>&`, and the value-type analogue).
  2. **Codegen**: assemble a runtime buffer -- push leading positionals (`&tmp`), append each unpacked container's elements (loop / `insert(end, span.begin(), span.end())`), push trailing positionals -- then `varargs<T>(buffer)`. Handle value-vs-ref element modes and multiple unpacks.
  3. **Lifetime (the awkward bit):** the buffer must be a **hoisted statement-level local**, NOT a GCC statement-expression (`({...; value;})`) -- the `varargs` holds pointers into the buffer, so if the buffer dies at the end of the statement-expression the view dangles. The literal-positional temps (`1`, `2`) must likewise outlive the call. This needs the codegen to emit prep statements before the call rather than a single initializer expression.

  Estimate ~0.5-1 day, medium risk (the buffer-lifetime pattern). Do it as its own scoped branch, not bolted onto star-unpack fixes. Surfaced by `/tpy-review` of `fix-star-unpack-generic-vararg`.
- **Star-unpack of an owning-rvalue / wrapped container is rejected.** `*make_items()` where the factory returns `Own[list[T]]` (or any `Own[...]`/`Ref[...]`-wrapped container) is cleanly rejected at sema with "Cannot unpack type 'Own[list[...]]' into *args" rather than supported. Earlier attempt to peel the wrapper in `_unpack_star_element_type` made sema accept it, but codegen then emitted `tpy::as_mut_span(<rvalue>)` which fails to compile (as_mut_span needs an lvalue span/vector reference, not a temporary). Supporting this needs codegen to materialize the owning rvalue into a frame/stack temp and span over that before packing. Workaround: bind to a local first (`xs = make_items(); f(*xs)`). Surfaced during `fix-star-unpack-generic-vararg`.
- **Double `analyze_expr(arg.expr)` for generic-vararg star-unpack.** A generic vararg call with `*xs` analyzes the inner container twice -- once in `_infer_arg_types` (inference) and again in `_analyze_and_pack_varargs` (packing). The shared `ExpressionAnalyzer.analyze_call_arg` helper unified the *logic* but not the two-pass structure. Harmless today (the second `analyze_expr` is a cached scope lookup for the common `TpyName` shape), but fragile if expression analysis ever gains non-idempotent side effects (borrow-tracking entries, flow-fact merge counters). Fix: have the packing pass consult the inference pass's cached type rather than re-analyze. Surfaced by `/code-review` of `fix-star-unpack-generic-vararg`.
- **[architectural cleanup] Unify call-argument analysis into one entry point.** Call arguments are analyzed at ~12+ scattered sites across `tpyc/sema/calls.py` and `methods.py` (generic-fn inference, the two overload-probe regimes, method-subst inference, pending-container/pending-generic-method paths, the per-builtin handlers, constructor fallbacks), each iterating `expr.args` and calling `analyze_expr` directly with no shared chokepoint that knows the callee signature. The `fix-star-unpack-generic-vararg` work reached *correct* star-unpack behavior but via a defense-in-depth patchwork rather than a design: (a) a `ExpressionAnalyzer.analyze_call_arg` helper that only the variadic-capable sites opt into; (b) a default-reject for `TpyStarUnpack` in `analyze_expr` as a *safety net* covering every site that doesn't opt in; (c) the "does not accept *args" reject duplicated at 3-4 sites (free-fn `_typecheck_call_args`, the generic non-variadic loop, the method dispatch, plus the analyze_expr net); (d) the variadic-element unwrap (`unwrap_readonly(unwrap_ref_type(span).type_args[0])`) now a 3rd copy of a pattern also in `type_ops.seed_arg_hint` / `infer_type_params_for_function`. A from-scratch design would have a single `analyze_call_args(expr, callee_signature)` that routes every call path, handling star-unpack per-position (element-extract at a variadic slot, reject otherwise) in one place -- which would let the safety-net reject and the duplicated gates be deleted, and would subsume the double-analyze item above. **This is NOT THIR-migration work**: call-arg analysis runs entirely in sema before THIR lowering, so the migration won't dissolve the scatter; folding this cleanup into THIR would only bloat it. Do it as its own deliberately-scoped sema refactor branch starting from the unified design, not as incremental edits. Surfaced by the multi-round review of `fix-star-unpack-generic-vararg`.
- **`_extract_awaitable_inner` doesn't substitute INT-kind type-params.** The fix at `tpyc/sema/expressions.py:_extract_awaitable_inner` (feat-gather-variadic) routes through `_substitute_type_params` from `tpyc/sema/operators.py`, which walks via `map_inner_types`. `NominalType.inner_types()` filters out INT-kind type-args, so a poll-shape carrying an INT type-param (e.g. `class MyAwait[T, N: int]: def __poll__(self, w) -> Own[Poll[Array[T, N]]]`) would leave `N` unsubstituted. No existing user has this shape; latent until a future generic awaitable carries an INT type param. Fix: replace the operators-side helper with `TypeOps.substitute_type_params` (handles INT slots explicitly) at the await-extraction site. Surfaced by `/code-review` of feat-gather-variadic.
- **Non-asyncio positive test for recursive `_extract_awaitable_inner` substitution.** The `tpyc/sema/expressions.py:_extract_awaitable_inner` fix that makes `list[T]` (and other nested generic shapes) substitute properly at the await-result-type inference site is currently only exercised by `tests/cases/async/asyncio_gather_varargs/`. A user-defined class with `def __poll__(self, w: Waker) -> Own[Poll[list[T]]]` (or `Poll[tuple[T, T]]` etc.) outside the asyncio stack would give the sema fix independent regression coverage. ~20 LOC under `tests/cases/async/` or `tests/cases/generics/`. Surfaced by `/tpy-review` of feat-gather-variadic.
- **`asyncio.gather_list` `return_exceptions=True`**. CPython's gather optionally collects exceptions into the result list (`list[T | BaseException]`) instead of cancel-and-re-raise. v1.5 M9 ships the default-False semantics only. Adding the kwarg-True path needs Box[Throwable] storage + a union-typed return list; ~30 lines on `_GatherFuture[T]`.
- **`Task.clone()` shared-TaskState semantics (multi-awaiter Task design).** v1.5 M9 added `Task[T].clone()` as a cheap Rc-bump used internally by `_GatherFuture[T]`. The clone aliases the same TaskState as the original handle, but `TaskState` is single-awaiter (one `awaiter: Waker` slot overwritten by each `__poll__`; one cached result slot consumed on first observation). Two real failure modes follow from any user who holds both the original Task and a clone: (a) **multi-awaiter alias** -- awaiting both concurrently (or sequentially when the first awaiter already consumed the result) overwrites/panics the second; e.g. `tasks=[t]; await gather_list(tasks); await tasks[0]` panics on `RuntimeError('Task: __poll__ after Ready was already consumed')`; (b) **cancel leak via shared TaskState** -- `_GatherFuture._propagate_cancel` cancels its clone, which routes through `TaskState.cancel_any()` and marks the user's original handle as cancelled too, surprising callers who didn't ask. The internal `Task.clone()` docstring carries a warning; the proper fix is a multi-awaiter `TaskState` (additive `awaiter_count` + waker list; result slot becomes ref-counted multi-consumer or "first consumer wins" panic moved into a typed `result_consumed` error). v2 scale -- not v1.5. Surfaced by /code-review of feat-asyncio-gather.
- **`@contextlib.contextmanager`**. Real user-convenience shortcut for cleanup-only context managers (post sync-`with` upgrade to 4-arg `__exit__`). Generator + try/finally + decorator pattern -- TPy has all three primitives. Probably ~30 lines of stdlib code or a class macro. Closes the ergonomics gap that bare 4-arg `__exit__` leaves for the common "I just want cleanup" case.
- **[correctness-fragility] `desugar_suspensions` compound traversal is a hand-maintained allowlist.** `_recurse_sub_bodies` / `_lower_stmt_exprs` walk a statement's `fields()` and then special-case the compound shapes whose await-bearing positions don't live in plain expr / stmt-list fields (try-handlers, `match` arm bodies, `with`-item context exprs). The canonical `exprs()` / `sub_bodies()` interfaces would be the natural traversal but are read-only (can't write the lowered expr back), so the pass mirrors `gen_async._map_compound_subbodies` instead. Risk: if a NEW compound node or await-bearing position is added later and not added to this enumeration, the failure mode is a *silently un-lowered await in a conditional / repeated position* -- the eval-order bug class this pass exists to fix, resurfacing in an unenumerated spot with no diagnostic. Fix: a writable visitor (map-with-rebuild over the canonical child interface) so await positions can't be missed by omission. Not urgent (enumeration is complete for today's node set); flagged so it isn't mistaken for cosmetic. Surfaced by the /tpy-ready retrospective second opinion.
- **`desugar_suspensions._has_await` re-scans subtrees.** `_lower` calls `_has_await(expr)` up front, then the per-construct branches call `_has_await` again on operands already known to contain a suspension (O(n^2) in chained-compare operand count / nesting depth). Not a practical cliff at current sizes, but folds out by threading a "contains-suspension" result down instead of re-scanning. Surfaced by /tpy-review (architecture-fit) of the await eval-order fix.
- **`await` inside a comprehension / generator expression**. Currently rejected cleanly by the pre-sema suspension desugar (`tpyc/parse/desugar_suspensions.py`) -- the `(prefix, value)` linearizer model doesn't fit a per-iteration suspension inside the comprehension's sub-scope. Full support means desugaring the comprehension to an explicit accumulation loop (`result = []; for x in xs: result.append(await f(x))`) before sema, including the `async for` comprehension form (`[x async for x in ait]`). Distinct from the eval-order desugar (which handles `and`/`or`/ternary/chained-compare/`while`-condition); this is a separate desugar-to-loop. Tests: `tests/cases/async/error_await_in_comprehension` guards the current reject.
- **[LOW prio, optimization] Share coro-frame sub-future slots via one variant.** Today each `await` site allocates its own `std::optional<__coro_X> __sub_N` frame field (`gen_async.py::_resumable_sub_future_fields`), so a function with N awaits carries N inline sub-coro slots even though they are never live simultaneously -- e.g. `await num() or await num() ...` (4 short-circuit lines) emits `__sub_0`..`__sub_7`, all `std::optional<__coro_num>` (see `tests/cases/async/await_short_circuit/expected/include/main.hpp`). Invariant that makes sharing sound: **at most one `__sub` is engaged per frame at any time** -- a coroutine parks at exactly one suspension point, and codegen resets the in-flight sub-future before advancing (and on the catch path); `create_task`/`gather` hold their own Rc/heap storage, not the caller's `__sub`. So one slot is the theoretical minimum and no liveness/interval analysis is needed. Cleanest shape: a single per-frame `std::variant<std::monostate, __coro_A, __coro_B, ...>` over the *distinct* sub-coro types (`monostate` = idle); the state machine knows the active type at each resume case, so polling is a static `std::get<__coro_X>(__sub).poll(waker)` (no `std::visit`, no dispatch cost), emplace via `__sub.emplace<__coro_X>(args)`, reset via `__sub.emplace<std::monostate>()`. The all-same-type case degenerates to a single-alternative variant (~optional).
