Caveats: dedup the alternative list (variant rejects duplicate types); slot size becomes max-alternative + tag (fine -- one slot is the floor); decide whether erased/boxed awaits (`await task` -> `unique_ptr<AsyncFrameBase<U>>`, a separate slot kind, also <=1-live) fold in as a pointer alternative or share one boxed slot; and do NOT fold in result slots (`__r_*` / hoisted locals) or `_lift_borrowed_rvalue_args` temps -- those genuinely overlap and stay separate. Recursive-async sizing is unchanged (same alternatives inlined as the optionals were). This is the concrete form of `docs/ASYNC_DESIGN.md` Open Question 6. Benefits both `async def` and (post-migration) generators -- but generators have no sub-futures, so async-only in practice. Frame-size win for await-heavy functions; not correctness.
- **Async borrow-checker hardening**. Two related lifetime gaps surfaced by the v1.5 control-flow lift (BUGS.md 202-205). Gap 1: `create_task(f(local_ref))` where `f` has reference-typed params captures by reference and the Task escapes the caller's scope -- dangling. Gap 2: borrowed-mode `await` on a temporary or short-lived reference-type awaitable. M3 (await-in-control-flow) ships with cheap mitigations: `_is_stable_lvalue` tightened to frame-fields-and-params only, and a sema warning on the escaping-create_task pattern. The real escape analysis (upgrade warnings to errors with proper call-graph tracking) is its own milestone, scheduled for after v1.5 completes (post-M6).
- **Runtime `type()` for exceptions**. v1.5's `__exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb) -> bool` always passes `exc_type = None` (sema rejects `exc_type is/== X` comparisons with a diagnostic pointing at `isinstance(exc_val, X)`). Real implementation needs class objects as first-class TPy values with a subclass-relationship table -- substantial sub-design touching the type system, runtime, and exception machinery. Unblocks: `exc_type is X` comparisons, `issubclass(exc_type, X)`, plus broader use of `type(x)` as a callable. Track as a separate language design item.
- **`@nomove` cost-refinement for inline-buffer types.** (The `@nomove` decorator itself now exists -- Phase 2 -- as "explicit non-movable": it sets `is_movable=False` so any relocation errors. What remains is the *cost-based* refinement below, for types that ARE movable but whose O(N) move the author wants made explicit.) Types with inline storage parameterized by N (`ArrayList[T, N]`, `Array[T, N]`, `FixStr[N]`) move in O(N) -- full element-by-element relocation, unlike `std::vector` whose move is a pointer-steal. Users who instantiate at large N can pay surprising costs at every implicit move site (return, `Own[T]` rebind, container reallocation). Surface: `@nomove class ArrayList[T, N]` declares "implicit moves not allowed; user must opt in via `copy()` at the call site -- be honest about the O(N) cost." Distinct from the `__move__` dunder (now Working): `__move__` *enables* an implicit relocating move (the O(N) cost is paid silently at return/reassign); `@nomove` is the opposite opt-out for an author who wants that cost made explicit via `copy()`. The two can coexist (a type whose move mechanism exists but whose author forbids implicit use). Open design points: (1) **NRVO-style elision** -- factory functions (`def make() -> ArrayList[T, N]: return ArrayList[T, N]()`) must still work; needs sema modeling of guaranteed copy/move elision so the trivial factory shape isn't rejected. This handling generalizes beyond `@nomove`; existing factory code benefits. (2) **Container storage** -- `list[NoMove]` reallocates via moves; needs a clean diagnostic pointing at the natural fix (`list[Box[NoMove]]`). (3) **Relation to `@nocopy`** -- orthogonal: a `@nomove` type can still be copy-constructible via `__copy__`, and `@nocopy` types like Box/Rc remain cheaply movable (pointer-steal). (4) **Diagnostic clarity** -- "implicit move of `@nomove` type would copy N elements; use `copy(x)` to make this explicit, or wrap in `Box[T]` for cheap moves" -- mirrors the existing "copies X into field" warning class.
- **[feature] Movability trait -- remaining relocation-site coverage (Phase 2 residuals).** Phase 2 shipped: movability as a propagated trait (`is_movable`, sibling to `is_send`/`is_sync`, with `RecordInfo.is_movable`/`move_override`/`has_move`, per-generic re-eval), a `why_not_movable` field-chain diagnostic (`tpyc/sema/move_chain.py`), the `@nomove` decorator (explicit, library-declared non-movable), codegen emitting `= delete` for non-generic non-movable `__del__` classes (so the class compiles; was a latent ill-formed member-wise move), and sema enforcement at by-value returns and `Own[tuple[...]]` per-element argument passing (via `require_movable` in `check_own_lvalue_into_own`). The compiler has ZERO knowledge of any specific library type: `UninitArrayStorage` is `@nomove` in its own stub (raw storage can't relocate itself), `ArrayList`/`FixStr` define `__move__`, and trivial fixed scratch buffers (e.g. `EpollReactor`'s epoll-output arrays) use the movable `Array[T, N]` rather than `UninitArrayStorage`. Consequence: an owner of `UninitArrayStorage` is non-movable for *any* element (no element-conditional free move) unless it defines `__move__`. Residuals: (1) **relocation-site coverage** -- plain `Own[T]` scalar call-arguments, last-use rebind (`q = p`), container insert, comprehension elements (a LIVE site since master's `owns_elements` comprehension-move landed), and tuple construction are NOT yet movability-checked in sema, so a non-movable type relocated there still surfaces as the raw C++ deleted-move error (for non-generic non-movable classes) or a deleted-`UninitArrayStorage`-move error (for generic instantiations). Wire `require_movable` into the remaining `is_auto_move_use` consumer sites, OR lift "this expr is a relocating move" into a single sema fact (e.g. `relocating_expr_ids`, parallel to `all_last_uses`) consumed by both the movability check and codegen's `std::move` emission -- the latter is the THIR-aligned end state (codegen stops independently deciding `_is_last_use_movable`). (2) **partial-drain leak** -- codegen unconditionally emits `<src>.__tpy_owned_ = false` after a `__move__` body and `_warn_unconsumed_own_params` blanket-skips `__move__`, so a user `__move__` that fails to drain every live slot silently leaks; consider verifying full drain or keeping the source dtor live for un-taken slots. (3) **indirect throw in `__move__`** -- a direct un-`try`-guarded `raise` in a `__move__` body is now a compile error (`_first_escaping_raise` in `registration.py`, `tests/cases/movability/error_move_raises`), but the move ctor is `noexcept` and `__move__` runs arbitrary user TPy, so an *indirect* throw (a callee that raises, an allocation) still yields a silent `std::terminate` with no definition-site diagnostic. Catching it needs nothrow tracking TPy lacks -- "warn on any call" is unworkable because the correct bodies call `relocate_from` (a call we can't distinguish as nothrow). Revisit if a `nothrow` marker / throw-propagation feature lands (or emit conditional noexcept). (4) **direct-call diagnostic** -- `x.__move__(y)` compiles under CPython but fails at C++ build with no TPy diagnostic; reject direct `__move__` calls in sema. (5) **`TriviallyRelocatable` bound + `relocate_trivial` intrinsic (general feature, deferred until a 2nd use case or perf pressure)** -- with `UninitArrayStorage` `@nomove`, every owner writes `__move__`, even for trivially-relocatable elements where it's a hand loop the optimizer should memcpy. A general compiler-derived `TriviallyRelocatable[T]` trait (NOT `ValueType` -- it must EXCLUDE BigInt and owned `std::string`; a conservative whitelist of fixed-width ints/bool/char/float/Ptr/views/tuples-of-those) would let a library `relocate_trivial[T: TriviallyRelocatable](dst, src, n)` primitive replace those hand loops, and could also gate a future memcpy-movable storage. Reusable beyond movability (serialization, native interop). Also: the C++ `UninitArrayStorage` move is still conditionally available (`requires is_trivially_copyable`) -- harmless dead code now (TPy never moves it), but could be unconditionally `= delete` to match the `@nomove` contract once the unchecked relocation sites in (1) are covered. (`has_move` on `RecordInfo`, also deferred from the Phase-1 review, shipped with Phase 2.) Inheritance: `__move__` on a class with a base that needs its own relocation is not yet handled (currently the trait walks parents structurally; explicit base-move chaining is untested). (6) **`@nomove` + `__move__` contradiction** -- a class declaring both is not rejected; codegen emits the custom `__move__` move ctor but suppresses move-assign (`nonmovable` gate), leaving it move-constructible-but-not-assignable (C++ Rule-of-5 implicit delete). Unreachable today (no class declares both). Reject the combination in sema: `__move__` *is* a movability declaration, so it contradicts `@nomove`. Surfaced building Phase 2.
- **[cleanup, now unblocked by `__move__`] Dogfood `UninitStorage[T]` as a pure-TPy class.** The single-slot owning storage (`tpy::UninitStorage<T>`, a `@native` C++ primitive) is now expressible in TPy: a `@nocopy` class over the `@nomove` `UninitArrayStorage[T, 1]` plus a liveness bool, with `__del__` and a `__move__` that transfers the live slot via `relocate_from(other._storage, 1)` -- correct for a non-trivially-relocatable payload, with the same nothrow constraint `relocate_from` already asserts. Before `__move__` this couldn't be written (no way to make a movable single-slot owner in TPy), so it's a genuine validation of the trait's generality. NOT worth doing casually: the consumers are the most ABI/bootstrap-sensitive primitives -- the `Rc` cell payload (`tplib/rc.py`, which caches a `Ptr` into `storage.ptr()` and is a generic `@dynamic` heap type with a careful layout), `Poll[T]` (`tpy/_core/_types.py`, one of the earliest-compiled modules -> bootstrap-order risk), plus channel send and the asyncio `Task`/`Future` result slots. It also doesn't reduce C++ much (`UninitArrayStorage` stays C++; you move one wrapper and gain a TPy `__move__`/bookkeeping body). Do it on its own branch, verifying Rc `ptr()`-stability + cell layout + the core-types bootstrap; likely needs `/tpy-add-feature` given it touches core primitives. Surfaced reviewing the Phase-2 shape.
- **[LOW]** Wrap the `make_unique<Adapter<P, ConcreteT>>(arg)` pattern into a `tpy::box_dyn<P>(arg)` runtime helper. Today every `Own[@dynamic-protocol]` call-arg wrap site (`_gen_dynamic_protocol_own_arg` in `tpyc/codegen_cpp/expressions.py:824-841`) emits the full `std::make_unique<::tpy::Adapter<P, std::remove_cvref_t<decltype(arg)>>>(arg)` spelling — readable enough but ~80 chars of boilerplate per site, especially noisy for async-def call args where `P` is `::tpystd::coro::Cancellable<...>`. A trivial header-only helper (`template<typename P, typename T> std::unique_ptr<P> box_dyn(T&& v) { return std::make_unique<Adapter<P, std::remove_cvref_t<T>>>(std::forward<T>(v)); }` next to `Adapter` in `runtime/cpp/include/tpy/dynamic.hpp`) lets codegen emit `::tpy::box_dyn<P>(arg)` instead. Purely cosmetic — same allocation, same template instantiation; one extra template-inline step the compiler folds away. Applies to *every* dyn-protocol wrap site (not just async), so the snapshot-regen diff would span all `@dynamic`-touching tests (`protocols/`, `async/`, plus a few in `inference/`, `readonly/`, etc.). Worth doing as a small standalone cleanup -- keep separate from any behavior-changing branch so the snapshot churn is isolated. Pairs with the structural-conformance branch (line 830) which can fold into the same helper. Surfaced during `feat-cancellable-async-typing` review.
- **[LOW]** Cut heap allocations on cancellable-API call sites by re-introducing a static-protocol cancellable shape for inline-holder consumers. After `feat-cancellable-async-typing` shipped, every `asyncio.run` / `create_task` / `wait_for` call emits `make_unique<Adapter<Cancellable<T>, ConcreteCoro>>(coro())` at the call site -- one heap alloc per call. The alloc count matches the pre-change `_box_coro` path (which boxed the same way, just hidden inside the stdlib helper), so the change is allocation-neutral; the optimization opportunity is reducing it. Two avoidable cases: (a) **`wait_for`-shaped inline holders** -- template `_WaitForFuture[T_aw, T]` over the concrete coro type (mirror of the `STATIC_PROTOCOL` `_CoroParamKind` machinery used for generic async methods today) so `_inner: T_aw` stores by value. Public signature stays `Own[Cancellable[T]]`; consumers become template-deduced. Trade-off: code size grows with the number of distinct coro types passed to `wait_for`. Implementation route: add a `STATIC_CANCELLABLE` shape paralleling `STATIC_PROTOCOL` but with a `Cancellable`-concept constraint (`__poll__` + `cancel`), or just make `Cancellable[T]` available in both `@dynamic` and non-`@dynamic` forms picked per consumer; (b) **`asyncio.run(main_coro)` main-task on stack** -- the main coro doesn't need the executor's slot table (which is for *spawned* tasks). Drive it via templated `poll_with_cancel` directly. ~30 lines of executor change, saves one alloc per `run()` call. The slot-table erasure for `create_task` is fundamental (heterogeneous container of `Box[AnyTask]`) and not in scope. Defer until allocation profiling actually surfaces this as a real hot path.
- **[interop] By-value struct parameters at a C boundary.** A C function taking `struct Rect` BY VALUE cannot be bound: a `@native(binding="C")` record renders `S&` in param position and `Own[S]` renders `S&&`, both C++ references with no C spelling, so the C-ABI gate rejects the shape and the only crossing that works is `Ptr[S]`. That is fine when the C side takes a pointer and useless when it does not -- and `extern "C"` does not mangle, so a user who "fixes" the diagnostic by switching to `Ptr[S]` against a by-value C definition gets a clean link and a callee reading a struct where an address was passed (the diagnostic now says so explicitly rather than steering them there). Needs a param form that renders the bare struct by value; the natural place is the same marshaling-wrapper design as the entry below, since a wrapper can spell the by-value parameter and forward.
- **[interop] Variadic C functions have no spelling.** The C-ABI gate rejects `*args` on a `binding="C"` function outright -- `*args` resolves to `varargs[T]`, a TPy template type that was previously emitted straight into the `extern "C"` declaration. The rejection closes a real hole but leaves no path: `printf`-style C functions cannot be bound at all. `docs/NATIVE_INTEROP.md` already lists variadic C support under "Future ideas" with the design open; this records that the gate has now made the gap explicit rather than silently wrong.
- **[interop] C-ABI marshaling wrappers -- let `str` / `bytes` / sequences cross a `binding="C"` boundary again.** The C-linkage type gate (`is_c_abi_allowed`, `tpyc/typesys.py`) rejects every type without a C spelling, so the manual `Ptr[readonly[uint8]]` + `unsafe_str_from_cstr` / `unsafe_cstr` recipe is the whole story today. The designed-but-deferred replacement is a WRAPPER, not an entry prologue: `@export(binding="C")` emits an ordinary namespaced function plus a generated `extern "C"` wrapper that marshals, and `@native(binding="C")` gets the symmetric inline forwarding wrapper on the import side. That shape is the only one that can express the two things a prologue cannot -- an ARITY-changing conversion (`bytes` -> `(const uint8_t*, size_t)`) and RETURN marshaling -- and it also keeps the cost off TPy-internal callers, who would bind the inner function directly and never touch the wrapper. What blocks it is a policy question rather than plumbing: who owns the buffer a `-> str` returns. `malloc` plus a documented free function, a thread-local static in the `strerror` mould, and a caller-supplied `(char* out, size_t cap)` pair (which changes the arity again) are all defensible and mutually exclusive -- decide before writing code. At that point the per-family conversion belongs on `TypeDef`, since the table would carry the conversion itself and not just the yes/no the gate needs today.
- **[interop] `@export(binding="C")` classes -- export a TPy class as a C struct.** Already listed as Planned in `docs/NATIVE_INTEROP.md` ("Classes (planned)"): an `extern "C"` struct with a C-compatible layout plus `Type_method(Type* self, ...)` free functions. Independent of the marshaling wrappers above -- it needs a layout and a naming rule, no conversion story -- and worth having first, because it strengthens the manual path: with it a user can spell a `{const uint8_t* data; size_t len;}` struct themselves and pass `Ptr[Buf]` through the C-linkage gate, which is exactly the shape a marshaling layer would otherwise have to generate.

## Ownership & Consuming Iteration
- **Container operations should accept MOVE-ONLY elements instead of demanding copy-constructibility.** `Rc[T]` is move-only by design with `clone()` as the explicit sharing path, but several container ops copy internally and so reject it outright: `reversed()` over a `list[Rc[T]]` and `list + list` both fail the C++ build on the deleted copy ctor (the two concrete shapes are filed in `BUGS.md`), and a dict KEY of `Rc[T]` is rejected outright (`Type 'Rc[P]' is non-copyable and cannot be used as a dict key; dict keys must be copy-constructible`) -- deliberate and clearly diagnosed, hence a design item here rather than a bug, but it is the shape that hurts most: an `Rc` handle is exactly what you want as an interned/shared key. (Dict VALUES of `Rc[T]` work; `heapq.heappush` fails earlier on type-argument inference, so audit the surface rather than trusting any enumeration of it.) The design question is the general one: which container ops can move internally, which should require an explicitly cloned value at the call site, and what the diagnostic says when neither applies (today it is raw libstdc++ spew). Getting this right is what makes `Rc` usable in the data structures shared ownership exists for. Surfaced by a downstream port.
- **`take()` builtin: move a value out of an Optional field, leaving `None` (Rust's `Option::take`).** Today a field read binds a borrow, so moving out of `x: T | None` (e.g. `conn = self._connection; self._connection = None; pool[k] = conn`) is rejected as a copy of a `@nocopy` type -- probe-verified during the keep-alive branch. `take(self.sock)` (or `self.sock.take()`) would move the payload out and backfill `None` atomically, the canonical idiom for owned-slot handoff. Known consumers waiting on it: `requests.Session._connection` seam -> pool routing, and the http.client will_close ownership-transfer redesign (below, Standard Library section) where `getresponse()` moves the transport into the response. Sibling consideration per feature discipline: the same shape applies to any owned-slot field (`Box | None`, `socket | None`, `SSLSocket | None`), and the design should say whether plain `T | None` unions and non-Optional owned fields (full-move + poison) are in or out of scope. Needs `/tpy-add-feature`.
- Consuming `items()` for dict: consuming `__iter__` works for keys, but consuming `items()` can't use `@overload` with `Own[Self]` because the return type changes (`dict_items` -> `Iterator[tuple]`), breaking non-iteration callers like `len(d.items())`. Needs a mechanism that only selects consuming dispatch when used as a for-loop iterable.
- `own_iter()` is list-only: kept as explicit escape hatch for non-last-use consuming. Could be made generic (dispatch to consuming `__iter__` on any type).
- `own()` builtin: explicit `T -> Own[T]` conversion (analogous to `span()` -> `Span[T]`).
- User-defined drain iterators (e.g. `ArrayListDrainIter`): view types with borrow tracking. See `docs/CONSUMING_ITERATION_DESIGN.md`.
- Codegen `std::move` for owned `self.field` returns: sema types `Own[Self].field` correctly as `Own[T]`, but codegen emits `return this->inner;` instead of `return std::move(this->inner);`. Breaks any `@nocopy` / unique-ownership field pattern with a C++ "use of deleted function X(const X&)" error from the copy path. Reproduces with `Own[Inner]` field + method body that mutates other state before `return self.inner`. Noted as "Partial" in `docs/CONSUMING_ITERATION_DESIGN.md` status table.
- [MED, feature, followup of the liveness exit-edges branch] **`with` suppression known before liveness.** Liveness takes every `with` as one whose `__exit__` may swallow an exception, because sema stamps `TpyWithItem.exit_can_suppress` only after the prescan. So a consume inside `with Plain(): take(p); p = P(5)` copies (warned), and the matching `@nocopy` program is rejected, although `Plain.__exit__` returns None and the exception always propagates. Removing that copy needs the manager expression's type (`Plain()`, `open(f)`, `self.lock`) before liveness runs: run liveness after the `with` items are resolved, or resolve them in an earlier pass. Needs `/tpy-add-feature`. The copies that stay are the required ones (a later statement may raise into a finally or handler that reads the value).
- [LOW, missed optimization; rejects-valid for `@nocopy`] Liveness takes every statement as one that may raise, and every `with` as one whose `__exit__` may swallow the exception (`tpyc/liveness.py`, the `_Exits.exc` landing): a consume followed by a statement that cannot raise (`p = None`, `n = 0`), or inside a `with` over a manager that never suppresses, copies (warned) where a move would be safe, once an exception path reads the name -- and a `@nocopy` value there is rejected ("is used after this point") although master compiles it: `with Cm(): if early: sink(p); return` then `sink(p)` after the `with`, `Cm.__exit__` returning None (probe `/tmp/agents/with_probe/main.py`). Measured 2026-09-25: no test snapshot pays it; kept by the user's choice over deciding suppression before the prescan. A try with a finally also gives every way out one shared landing (the finally walked from all of them; only a return's own names stay apart), so a consume before a `break` whose loop header reads the name copies although the `break` path does not: per-kind landings are precise but cost a finally walk per exit kind, exponential in nesting, until MIR. Moving there needs a proven-nonthrowing statement whitelist, and the manager's `__exit__` known before the prescan (the manager expression's type, not only the method signature).
- [LOW, missed optimization] A consume of a `for` loop's own iterable inside the body copies on every path out, a `return` or `break` included (`for x in xs: return take(xs)` renders a `__tmp` copy and warns): the move gate (`BorrowTracker.has_borrowers_outside`) honours the iteration loan for the whole body, while on a leaving path nothing advances the iterator again and only a still-live loop variable or element borrow holds `xs`. Moving there needs the loan to end where the iterator's last use is -- a liveness fact about the hidden iterator, the MIR borrow-region question, not a sema special case.
- [LOW, missed optimization] `borrow_reassigned_vars` is an add-only accumulator: a local that cycles owned -> borrow-alias -> owned-again stays barred from the movable set, so its final consume copies instead of moving. Safe (a copy is always sound for reference types), but pessimises that rare pattern. A precise fix would discard from the set on re-ownership, but that reintroduces the flow-sensitivity the union accumulator avoids -- defer until the THIR place/loan model makes per-binding movability natural.
- [LOW, missed inlining] The out-of-line ctor size partition (`records.py` `_gen_ctor_def`) counts the RAW `__init__` body, but field-init assigns hoist into the MIL -- a pure-field-init ctor with >7 `self.x = x` lines lands non-inline in the `.cpp` although its emitted def is a trivial `R::R(...) : a(a), ... {}` MIL one-liner, losing cross-TU inlining on a hot path. Count the post-hoist residue instead (needs the hoist decision earlier, or a cheap "simple self-field assign" pre-count). Surfaced by the /tpy-ready retrospective of the ctor out-of-line fix.
- [LOW, cleanup] `_store_analysis_results` (`sema/analyzer.py`) computes the exported movable set as a 3-clause exclusion cascade over `ever_owned_locals` (skip hoisted, skip reassigned+lvalue_reassigned, skip borrow_reassigned). Consolidate the exclusion sources into a single `never_movable_locals` set built incrementally as statements are analyzed, so the post-pass filter collapses to `ever_owned - never_movable` and a future exclusion reason is single-site. Aligns with the THIR direction (per-place movability); defer until then.

## Build pipeline
- **[test-flake] `tpyc/test_build_cache.py::test_record_after_compile_no_edit_hits` is flaky on the remote pytest host, passing locally.** Observed twice on 2026-07-31, different branches, in full `rpytest` runs; both times a local rerun of the file (and once a clean remote rerun) passed 22/22. `check_up_to_date` returns None right after `_compile_and_record`, i.e. some manifest input reads as changed on the remote tmpdir -- suspicion: mtime granularity/skew on the remote filesystem (`/srv/fast` tmp). Diagnose by dumping WHICH manifest entry mismatches on failure (the check has a reason path); consider stamping mtimes explicitly in the test fixture. Unrelated to the branches it surfaced on (neither touched build_cache). Per-eval cost today is ~0.8s entry-TU compile (g++ + PCH) + ~0.1s link; measured levers, in increasing value: (a) `-fuse-ld=mold` when detected (link 70ms -> 20ms on a small object set; grows with session object count); (b) ccache on the REPL's support-object compiles (kills the first-eval bulk cost across sessions -- generated TUs churn per eval and don't benefit); (c) the real fix: the clang-repl JIT backend (~20-80ms/expr, 10-40x) -- needs clang-repl >= 19 (std::expected; the batch-side floor is enforced by the toolchain capability probe in tpyc/toolchain.py) AND the managed-libs/runtime-impls gap closed by loading a prebuilt support `.so` into the interpreter (BUGS.md clang-repl entry). Compiler shopping is NOT a lever: clang++ is only ~12-14% faster than g++ at -O0 on the runtime-shaped workload (measured 2026-07-03), and PCH flattens most of that. Surfaced by the REPL-latency question after fix-repl-managed-libs.
- **[cleanup] REPL PCH cache dir bypasses shared_cache_root().** `tpyc/repl_backends.py` hardcodes `Path.home()/".cache"/"tpyc"` for its PCH cache, ignoring the `$TPYC_SHARED_CACHE_DIR` override and Windows %LOCALAPPDATA% path that `tpyc.toolchain.shared_cache_root()` (the single derivation, shared with the test harness and the toolchain probe cache) honors. Pre-existing; route it through the shared helper. Surfaced by /tpy-review (architecture-fit) of toolchain-preflight.
- **[design] Managed-dep granularity: `datetime`'s tz backend is linked (and gated by `--date`) even for pure-calendar use.** `lib/tpy/datetime.py` imports `_bindings.hinnant_date` at module level, so `from datetime import timedelta` -- pure calendar math with zero OS dependency, which worked dep-free in v1 -- now links tz.cpp + date_shim.cpp into the binary, and `--date=none` turns ANY datetime import into a compile error. For `re`->pcre2 / `ssl`->mbedtls the dep is intrinsic to the whole module; datetime is the first managed lib where half the surface doesn't need the backend. Options: (a) document-and-accept (a note in DATETIME_DESIGN.md's backend section records the coupling); (b) link a managed dep only when one of its `@native` symbols is actually referenced by the compiled program (general dead-dep elimination -- pairs with the existing "do not compile .cpp files that are not needed" item below); (c) split the wall-clock surface into a submodule imported on use (fights CPython's single-module shape). Needs `/tpy-add-feature` if (b)/(c). Surfaced by the /tpy-ready second-opinion retrospective of datetime v2.
- **Stop writing the legacy `libtpy`/`runtime` session-fingerprint keys.** `tests/.session_fingerprints.json` still records both keys although (per CLAUDE.md) they no longer gate any phase -- every branch churns them on the first local run, producing recurring pure-noise commits and cross-branch merge conflicts (datetime-v2 alone carried two churn commits + one merge conflict on this file). Drop the writers (and the keys) in conftest; `cpy_stubs` stays. Surfaced by the /tpy-ready retrospective of datetime v2.
- **[nit] Rename the third-party `c_sources` plumbing to `third_party_sources`.** The field/params (`ThirdPartyBuildPlan.c_sources`, `build_cpp_commands(c_sources=...)`, conftest's `third_party_c_sources`) now carry `.cpp` files too (Hinnant date; driver picked per suffix by `third_party_source_driver`); comments are accurate but the names lie. Mechanical rename across compiler.py/cli.py/conftest.py. Surfaced by the /tpy-ready second-opinion retrospective of datetime v2.
- **Test harness: a pytest `--release` mode building the exec phase at `-O3`.** The suite compiles every case with `opt_flags=[]` (no `-O`, no `-g`, `NDEBUG` undefined) and never through the CLI's default, so the optimizer never sees the corpus -- an optimizer-exposed UB sweep (a dangling reference the `-O0` build happens to tolerate) has no harness form. Needs the opt flags in the shared PCH-cache key (the `conftest.py` comment above `get_pch_header` warns exactly this: today the PCH is valid only because `opt_flags` is always empty) and in the exec-result marker key so a `--release` pass does not mark the debug marker green (or vice versa). Filed from the CLI optimized-default design pass; `tpy`'s default is `-O3` since then while the suite stays unoptimized by design.
- **Test harness: link only the imported stdlib `.o` per case (exec-cache precision).** Today every case links the WHOLE precompiled stdlib `.o` set (`precompiled_objects=cache.objects`) with no `--gc-sections`, so an unimported module is still in the binary. The exec fingerprint therefore folds in `stdlib_output_hash` (the full set's identity) to stay sound -- which means any stdlib-codegen change re-keys EVERY case. If instead a case linked only the `.o` for the modules it imports (its `all_modules` stdlib entries, which are the transitive import closure), the link-set would equal the hashed-set: the `stdlib_output_hash` term could drop, giving full per-case cache precision (a stdlib edit re-verifies only the cases that actually use the changed module). Risks to design through `/tpy-add-feature`: transitive C++ symbol deps that don't map 1:1 to TPy imports (under-link -> undefined-symbol link errors), and bundled C deps (PCRE2 `.o`) that are separate objects needing inclusion when their module is imported. Pure optimization (current design is sound); do it on its own branch. Surfaced by /tpy-ready on the exec-cache branch.
- **Test coverage: cross-module-cycle records with `__del__`/`__copy__` are unwitnessed.** The out-of-line special-member emission forces cycle members' dtor/move/copy defs into the `.cpp` (`records.py` def-mode `cycle_peers` gates); intra-module and size-driven partitions are covered (`records/recursive_record_mutual_{del,copy}`), but no case combines a cross-module record cycle with `__del__`/`__copy__`. Needs a two-module cycle fixture like `imports/mutual_cycle_record_reexport` plus special members. Surfaced by /tpy-review of the ctor out-of-line fix.
- **Test harness: no automated test for the exec-phase UX (`--no-exec`, the exec tally, the start-of-run cause line).** The soundness-critical `compute_exec_fingerprint` is unit-tested (`tests/test_exec_fingerprint.py`), but the plugin behaviors that sit on top of it are only manually verified: `--no-exec` skips exec while keeping cpy + its mutual-exclusion guard; the `tpy| exec: N built+run, M skipped` terminal tally (incl. xdist worker->controller aggregation via `workeroutput`); the `report_exec_env_change` cause line (fires on a shared-input change, suppressed under forced modes, per-checkout record). Cover with pytest's `pytester` fixture (in-process sub-pytest runs asserting on stdout) -- low priority; these are dev-tooling, not compiler behavior. Surfaced by /tpy-ready on the exec-cache branch.
- **Test harness: `test_build_cache_lifecycle` fails under whole-suite cold-cache contention.** `tests/test_build_cache_cli.py` runs a program twice and asserts the second run hits the warm path (`assert not built_cold(...)`); it does, in isolation on both the local and the remote build host. It FAILED once in a full-suite run whose exec cache had just been fully invalidated by a master merge (`tpy| exec: 3630 built+run, 0 skipped via cache`) and passed in the immediately following run against a warm cache (`3604 skipped`). So the second (warm) `tpyc` invocation rebuilds when ~3600 other cases are concurrently compiling against the shared stdlib `.o` / PCH / ccache. Nothing in the compiler is implicated (a branch touching no `build_cache.py` / `cli.py` / `toolchain.py` reproduced it). Either the test needs isolation from that contention (its own cache root, or xdist-serialized), or the warm-path check needs to distinguish "manifest miss" from "shared cache evicted underneath us" -- worth knowing which, since the second would be a real cache-soundness gap rather than a test artifact. Surfaced by /tpy-ready on `fix-dead-rebind-slots`.
- **Test harness: a failed stdlib pre-compilation empties the shared cache with no end-of-run signal.** `_setup_stdlib_cache` catches the compile `RuntimeError`, `_log`s a stderr warning and returns an empty `_StdlibCache`; `get_stdlib_cache` then falls through to the ephemeral path, which rebuilds and fails identically, so the run warns twice at session start and every case recompiles the stdlib for the rest of the run. Both warnings scroll off in a long run, and the only remaining symptom is slowness -- which is exactly what hid the cross-checkout PCH collision until someone profiled it. The degradation itself is deliberate (a broken stdlib TU must not abort the suite), so the fix is surfacing, not raising: add a `tpy| stdlib cache: DEGRADED (<reason>)` line to `terminal_summary`, mirroring the existing STALE FINGERPRINTS banner. Surfaced by the /tpy-ready retrospective of the PCH cache-key fix.
- when a module forwards imports only, those imports should not generate headers if the symbols are not used
- do not compile .cpp files that are not needed, e.g. no function is called etc
- **(low prio) Route CLI builds through the shared PCH/stdlib cache.** `tpy file.py` builds up to three PCH variants (~160MB each: plain + `debug/` + `release/`) plus stdlib objects into every program's `__tpyc__/<prog>.d/`, so a hello-world build dir weighs ~480MB and a dozen built example programs ~3.5GB. The test harness already solved this -- shared, content-addressed PCH + stdlib `.o` in `~/.cache/tpyc` (see conftest's `get_stdlib_cache` / `get_pch_header`); the CLI path (`compiler.get_or_build_pch`, which stores the PCH "inside the build output directory") never adopted it. Re-plumb the CLI to the shared cache with the same invalidation keys (runtime-header hash, compiler identity, flags, and -- on any compiler where `toolchain.pch_is_path_sensitive` holds -- the checkout's runtime include root, without which two checkouts collide on one .gch; note the existing gap too: the current staleness check compares only header mtimes, see BUGS-adjacent note in the PCH-cache entry of the audit). Per-program build dirs then shrink to generated sources + objects + binary. `/tpy-add-feature`-shaped: cache keying and concurrent-build locking need a design pass.
- **(low prio) Registry-drive the managed-third-party CLI wiring.** Four managed libs (`pcre2`, `mbedtls`, `date`, `zlib`) now each cost an argparse `--<lib>` registration in `cli.py`, an entry in `cli.THIRD_PARTY_LIBS` (which builds both mode dicts -- the build-cache key and the build plan -- and which `tpyc/test_third_party_zlib.py` pins to the registry), and a `_FACTORIES` row. The flag name and default already live on `ThirdPartyLib`; moving the help text there too would let `cli.py` register the flags in a loop, leaving `_FACTORIES` the single source of truth -- without importing the build layer on the warm build-cache path (the reason `THIRD_PARTY_LIBS` is a literal). Surfaced by /tpy-review (architecture-fit) of the mbedTLS and zlib wiring.
- **(low prio) Share the third-party build boilerplate.** `tpyc/build/{pcre2,mbedtls,date,zlib}.py` each carry the same read-the-sidecar-manifest-and-verify loop (only the subdirectory differs; a `manifest_source_files(lib, manifest_name, subdir)` helper next to `read_source_manifest` would absorb it), and `scripts/vendor_*.py` each copy `_sha256` / `_download` / the sidecar read/stamp/write and the idempotent `main` (a `scripts/_vendor_common.py`). Surfaced by /tpy-review (architecture-fit) of the zlib vendoring.
- **(low prio) De-duplicate the vendor-script sidecar helpers.** `scripts/vendor_cacert.py`, `vendor_mbedtls.py`, and `vendor_pcre2.py` now carry a verbatim-identical `_stamp` / `_read_sidecar` / `_read_sidecar_version` / `_write_sidecar` shape (nothing lib-specific in the timestamp-reuse + sidecar-read logic). A shared `scripts/_vendor_common.py` with `stamp(sidecar_path, metadata)` / `read_sidecar(path)` would remove the triplication without disturbing the documented "one vendor script per lib" pattern. Threshold now met: the fourth vendor script (`vendor_date.py`, datetime v2) landed as another verbatim copy -- fold in on the next vendoring touch. Surfaced by /tpy-review (architecture-fit) of the bundled CA store.
- **Fill in package metadata before public release.** `pyproject.toml` declares only `name`/`description`/`Homepage = https://tpy.dev`. Add `authors`/`maintainers`, a `Repository` URL (deferred while the GitHub repo is private), and a `license` field + `LICENSE` file (project is currently unlicensed = all-rights-reserved; pick proprietary vs OSS when going public). Optionally `keywords` + trove `classifiers` for PyPI discoverability.
- **[feature] pyproject v0: build TPy extensions and apps from pyproject.toml.** Two user stories: (a) a `# tpy: ext_module` builds into the user's wheel as part of a normal pyproject build (PEP 517 hook or build-backend plugin wrapping `tpyc -b`); (b) a standalone TPy app builds/installs from its pyproject (entry point -> compiled binary). v1 deliberately minimal (a `[tool.tpy]` table + a build hook), but the DESIGN must be forward-looking -- dependency consumption (TPy libraries installed as PyPI packages on the compiler search path) and the `tpx` porcelain (docs/PROJECT_TOOLING_DESIGN.md) should be extensions of the same shape, not a second mechanism. Own `/tpy-add-feature` design pass before building. Scoped for 0.6.0 (RELEASE_PLAN).
- **[feature] Per-project compilation options in pyproject (`[tool.tpy]`).** Today project-wide options (`--default-int`, third-party lib modes; future: range-check mode, string/char representation) live on the CLI invocation only; tests use options.json. Users need a committed per-project home so builds are reproducible without wrapper scripts: read `[tool.tpy]` from the nearest pyproject.toml, explicit CLI flags override. Design together with the pyproject v0 build hook (same table, one discovery rule). Scoped for 0.6.0 (RELEASE_PLAN).

## Compiler Performance / mypyc

Goal: speed up test runs (currently ~3 min parallel, ~6 min single-threaded for non-slow tests) and prepare for self-hosting. These optimizations are worth doing independently but also remove mypyc blockers.

### Hotspot fixes (ordered by impact)

- Memoize type transformations: parked. PERF TODO note left at `substitute_type_params` in `sema/type_ops.py` for the next candidate; needs profiling data post-mypyc before acting.
- `isinstance` overhead on type predicates: `TypeKind` / `TpyType.tag` was retired when primitive subclasses collapsed to `NominalType` singletons; predicates now dispatch through `type_def_of(t).category` (dict lookup + attribute) or compound isinstance for structural types -- a per-call cost regression vs the prior frozenset tag lookups. Real win lands under mypyc; pre-mypyc profiling hasn't been done. Pre-mypyc mitigations noted as `PERF TODO` comments at the hot paths (`coercions.py::resolve_coercion`, `type_def_registry.py::type_def_of`, `typesys.py::is_numeric_type` family) -- hash-table coercion dispatch and per-instance category caching on `NominalType` are the two concrete knobs if a profile shows the dispatch is bottlenecking.

### mypy compliance (~1086 errors remaining)

- `TypeGuard` on predicate helpers (`is_protocol_type` -> `TypeGuard[NominalType]`, etc.) -- ~86 `attr-defined` errors
- `Scope | None` union-attr errors (67) -- genuinely optional, needs per-site narrowing
- `arg-type` (448), `assignment` (175) -- scattered, per-file mechanical work
- `object.__setattr__` in `PtrType.__post_init__` -- refactor to avoid

### mypyc integration (after mypy compliance)

- switch from hatchling to setuptools with mypyc build step (or mypycify)
- keep macro loader as pure Python, exclude from mypyc compilation

## Investigate
- Unify the two inherited-subst composition copies into one shared helper (e.g. `type_ops.compose_type_substs`): `tpyc/sema/methods.py` `_analyze_instance_method` composes inherited x instance substs one level (with an `isinstance(v, TpyType)` guard for `N: int` bindings), while `tpyc/sema/protocols.py:740-758` has a more complete twin that also transitively resolves `TypeParamRef` chains. Hand-converged duplicates drift. While unifying, verify multi-hop generic-through-generic chains with a test (`class Mid[V](Bag[V, 8]); class Leaf[W](Mid[W])` -- the flat merge in `lookup_record_method_overloads` plus one-level composition may leave the declaring param bound to the intermediate one; unverified, surfaced by /tpy-review of the subclass-receiver bound fix).
- Polymorphic integer literals (Rust-style). A function local whose first binding is a bare literal is now typed by the values stored in it ("Pending integer locals" below); uses never decide a type, so `a = 0; f(a)` for `f(x: uint64)` still needs `a: uint64 = 0` or a cast (the mismatch names the annotation). Not covered: module-level constants (`CONST = 5`) and collection-element literals (`weights = [10, 20, 30]; send_byte(weights[0])`). Letting a literal adapt to a typed USE everywhere would reopen the order question the pending locals settled (every sema site reading a local's type mid-flow would have to handle "still a literal"), and needs a generic-inference policy for a literal argument binding `T`. Defer until real code asks for it.
- CPython native (C) module for tpy stubs: the `lib/cpy/tpy/` stubs are pure Python. A C extension module could improve CPython performance for programs that use tpy types (int32, Array, Span, etc.) heavily.
- investigate rust like feature (borrowing, lifetimes etc) to make the language safe; however these should be softer restrictions than in rust
- zig language: what it is, how is it different from C, what useful patterns can we learn
- Distinct types (newtypes): `class Meters(Distinct[float]): pass` -- zero-cost wrapper that creates a nominally distinct type. Prevents mixing incompatible values of the same underlying type (units, IDs, currencies). C++ codegen: thin struct wrapper or strong typedef. Inspired by Nim's `distinct` keyword.
- `@constexpr` decorator: mark pure functions as compile-time evaluable, emit C++ `constexpr`. Useful for lookup tables, constants, config. Low implementation cost -- lean on C++ compiler. `TABLE: Final[int32] = factorial(10)` computed at compile time.
- Inline iterators: `@inline` on generator functions to unroll the loop body at the call site instead of creating a state machine. Zero overhead, important for hot paths. Generalizes what `range()` already does implicitly to user-defined iterators. Inspired by Nim's inline vs closure iterator distinction.
- Runtime exception migration -- see `docs/EXCEPTION_DESIGN.md` for the per-type migration table (status, sites, divergences). Pending items live there, not here.
- Better runtime panic message for unhandled `@error_return` calls. Currently `_maybe_error_return_unwrap` (`tpyc/codegen_cpp/expressions.py`) emits `tpy_panic("unhandled error return")` which is opaque -- doesn't include the function name or the error value's data. Improve to `tpy_panic("unhandled X in <func>: " + e.message)` or similar. Affects all return-tier panic sites uniformly.

## Builtins
- **Builtin combinators in TPy source (`enumerate`, `filter`; later `zip`, `reversed`, `map`).** `enumerate`/`zip`/`filter`/`map`/`reversed` are C++ runtime iterators (`runtime/cpp/include/tpy/itertools.hpp`). Since 2026-09-22 they hand an element on in the form their SOURCE steps it (`detail::range_elem` / `step_member_t` / `result_step_t`): a container lends with its const, an iterator's lent step is lent on, a fresh value is owned -- deduced in C++ off the source, with the compiler naming no SOURCE element type (the `<T>` template arguments are gone from the stubs; `map` keeps its declared `<U>`, the callable's return being the compiler's own fact), so the copying entries this direction was opened for are closed and the comprehension route's name-keyed fence is gone. What is left of the case for TPy-source combinators is the one-rule argument (the yield-form rule the compiler owns at a `yield` restated, now by deduction, in the runtime) against the measured perf gap below. **Direction (chosen 2026-09-13; re-weighed 2026-09-22 after the runtime fix, still open):** write them as ordinary TPy generators in `lib/tpy`, so the yield-form rule decides the element form once, in the compiler. A feasibility probe wrote all five and their consumers (`/tmp/agents/probe_tpy_combinators/`: `p_enum.py`, `p_map.py`, `p_filter.py`, `p_rev.py`, `p_zip*.py`, plus the `nest_*.py` nesting consumers); the bodies are a few lines each and compile today except where the prerequisites below bite. **Pilot order:** `enumerate`, `filter` -- `map` is DEFERRED to TODO.md "Callable contract": until the callable's declared return carries its ownership, a TPy-source `map` cannot follow a borrow-returning `fn`, and the C++ one's call-site inference already does. The C++ `zip` and `reversed` stay until their own prerequisites land. **Prerequisites,** by slug: the enabling mechanism -- a generic generator's yield form decided per instantiation, so a TPy-source combinator lends its elements -- LANDED 2026-09-17; what a combinator yields through an erased `Fn` still copies (BUGS.md#generic-yield-fn-result-copies), which is the same reason `map` is deferred below. BUGS.md#frame-try-next-error-return-miscompiles for `zip`'s two-iterator driver, or instead admitting `ia = iter(a)` in the protocol-param alias rule so `zip` can be written over `Iterable` params at all (today both spellings reject: the `Iterable`-param one at the alias rule, the `Iterator`-param one at the `try`); BUGS.md#subscript-elem-record for `reversed`'s borrowing `yield seq[i]`; a readonly-source form -- both spellings reject today, `readonly[Iterable[T]]` with a plain `T` yield at sema (*Cannot pass readonly[T] as mutable T in yield value*) and the `readonly[T]` element yield at THIR (`sgen.tuple_yield_source`), probes `p_nest_ro.py` / `p_nest_ro2.py`; BUGS.md#comp-unpack-pointer-tuple-skips-deref and BUGS.md#collect-pointer-tuple-into-storage-vector for the tuple-yielding ones consumed by a comprehension or `list()`; BUGS.md#dispatch-generator-pair-sema-crash plus a `T: Truthy` bound for the `filter(None, it)` variant; and a pending list literal at a `Sequence[T]` slot (`my_reversed([1, 2, 3])` -> *Type PendingList[...] does not conform to protocol Sequence[int32]*; the `str` literal already conforms). **Perf (measured, `p_perf_*.py`, 10M elements x 10 reps):** a peephole-shaped TPy body runs at 1.0x the C++ builtin (`enumerate`), a resumable-frame body at ~2.2x on a tight int loop (`filter`, whose `if` in the loop body routes it to the frame) -- so either widen the peephole to cover these shapes, or accept the gap for `filter`/`zip`. No variadic type params, so `zip` is a per-arity `@dispatch` set rather than one definition.
- **[cleanup] The per-element source map of a tuple-yielding iterator (`_yield_elem_sources`, `tpyc/sema/iter_loans.py`) is derived at every tuple-unpack `for` site from the callee's generic signature; the whole-return fact (`return_borrows_from`) for the same callee is stamped once at registration.** Decide it once, beside `return_borrows_from` (a per-element index map on `FunctionInfo`), so the `it = zip(xs, ys); for a, b in it` binding position gets it too once that shape routes. Same file: the free-function and method finalize blocks in `tpyc/sema/analyzer.py` stamp three mutation lattices in two hand-kept copies -- one `_finalize_mutation_facts` before a fourth fact arrives.
- **[cleanup] One per-element provenance walk instead of two.** `iteration_elem_provenance` (the owning-slot copy warning's STRICT reading: a type-param element comes only from the operands whose parameter mentions that param) and `_yield_elem_sources` (the tuple-unpack `for`'s WHOLE-VARIABLE reading: an element with no named source falls back to every operand) both walk `tpyc/sema/iter_loans.py`'s `iterated_storage` operands against the callee's generic signature. Beyond that flag they differ in two ways, and that is where the tuple-unpack `for`'s loans and the copy warning disagree: `iteration_elem_provenance` counts the RECEIVER (index -1) as a source of a type-param element, and RECURSES into a nested lending call (`zip(filter(keep, cs), xs)`, whose `C` element takes the inner call's own per-element provenance); `_yield_elem_sources` does neither -- it keys only positional parameters and takes a nested call's operand as its flat roots. Merge them into one walk with a strict/whole-variable flag, so a new combinator shape is taught once; the per-`FunctionInfo` index map in the entry above is where the merged walk's signature half would live.
- **[cleanup] Decide "the callee retains its arguments past the statement" once.** The fact is spelled inline as `frame_factory_callee(fi) or fi.is_async` at three sites -- the THIR method-call argument hoist and the free-call `frame_capturing` verdict (`tpyc/thir/lower/expressions.py`), and sema's `call_lend_sources` temp-backing gate and `frame_borrowed_operands` (`tpyc/sema/context.py`) -- while `temp_arg_kept_alive` (`tpyc/sema/iter_loans.py`) asks `frame_factory_callee` alone, so a coroutine's temporary argument the lowering hoists is not counted as kept alive by the dangle warnings. Name the fact once in `tpyc/value_category.py` beside `frame_factory_callee` and read it at every site; aligning `temp_arg_kept_alive` changes which warnings fire, so it is a decision, not a refactor.
- **[cleanup] The deferred generic-yield settle (the per-instantiation yield form the entry above rests on) retains whole ANALYSIS CONTEXTS, and mutates them.** `ctx.deferred_generic_yield_settles` (`tpyc/sema/context.py`) parks a `(TpyFunction, FunctionTrackingState)` pair per generic generator until the end of the module's `analyze_bodies`, and `_settle_deferred_generic_yields` (`tpyc/sema/analyzer.py`) then writes to each parked state -- it reinstalls `current_function` and clears `pending_generic_yield_sources` -- so the field's own "nothing mutates it once the body is done" note is already false. Record the FACTS the verdict walk needs (the yield sources, plus the params / scope / frame locals it roots them against) instead of retaining the analysis context.
- **`min(iterable)` / `max(iterable)` single-iterable form.** Only the variadic `min(a, b, ...)` form exists today; `min(xs)` over a `list`/iterable -- the *primary* Python usage -- errors with "No matching overload for min(list[int32])". Add the iterable-reducing overload (and `key=`/`default=` to follow). Common first-non-trivial-program idiom. Surfaced by /tpy-fuzzy-test (collections), 0.3.0 smoke test. **Re-reported downstream 2026-08-03 and still live** (`max(xs)` over `list[float]` -> `No matching overload for max(PendingList[float, 3]#0)`), called out there as a P0 builtin and "one of the most common shapes in ordinary Python"; they worked around it with `sorted(xs)[-1]`. Two independent reports plus a trivial workaround-with-a-sort is the signal to schedule this rather than leave it in the backlog.
- **`reverse=` keyword on `list.sort()`.** `sorted(xs, reverse=True)` works since 2026-10-02; `xs.sort(reverse=True)` is still refused (*'sort' got unexpected keyword argument 'reverse'*). Add the keyword to the method stub and its runtime. Surfaced by /tpy-fuzzy-test (collections), 0.3.0 smoke test.
- **`key=` keyword on `list.sort()`.** `xs.sort(key=lambda c: c.k)` fails with `'sort' got unexpected keyword argument 'key'` (over records the earlier `Comparable` check fires first). `sorted(key=...)` exists; `list.sort` should take the same `key` (and the `reverse=` above). Surfaced by the tte example port.
- **`int(text, base)` two-argument form.** `int("ff", 16)` fails with `int() takes (0, 1) arguments, got 2`. Hex/binary parsing is a first-page idiom (the tte port hand-rolls a hex-digit lookup for colors).
- **Builtins as first-class function values.** `key=len`, `key=abs` etc. fail with "'len' is not a variable" -- builtin FUNCTION names can't be passed as callables (only user `def`s can). Builtin CLASS names can (`map(str, xs)`, `key=int`, `Callable[[], list[int]] = list`: a class name at a callable slot is `lambda *a: C(*a)`, see LANGUAGE_FEATURES "Class names as callable values"); a builtin function is a different binding (an overload set with native renders, often special-cased sema), so it does not ride that expansion. The diagnostic should at least suggest wrapping (`def my_len(s: str) -> int32: return len(s)`); the feature is making builtin references materialize as callable values. Surfaced by /tpy-fuzzy-test (collections), 0.3.0 smoke test.
- **Fold `int()` / `float()` / `str()` with no arguments to the literal at a typed slot.** `int()` at an `int32` slot builds a `::tpy::BigInt` and range-checks it (`(::tpy::BigInt()).to_fixed_check<int32_t>()`), the same render `def f() -> int32: return int()` has; `float()` at a `float` slot and `str()` at a `str` slot build the default the same way. The factory spelling makes it hot: `defaultdict[str, int32]` with factory `int` (a class name at a `Callable[[], int32]` slot is `lambda: int()`) builds and checks a `BigInt` per missing key. Folding a no-argument builtin value-class construction to the literal of the slot's type (`0`, `0.0`, `""`) removes it at every position at once; decide it where the call's type is decided (sema), not in the render.
- **A function or class name at an OVERLOADED METHOD's `Fn`/`Callable` parameter.** `c.conv(parse, "41")` and `c.conv(int, "41")`, where `conv` is a method with two `@dispatch` variants taking different `Callable` shapes, fail with "'parse' is not a variable": the method overload path analyzes the arguments before a candidate is chosen and drops the callable hint for a name (`tpyc/sema/methods.py`, the probe-args loop), with no per-candidate trial. A lambda argument fails there too ("Lambda parameter types cannot be inferred without context"). The free-function path has a per-candidate trial (regime C, `CallAnalyzer._resolve_regime_c`) that takes a lambda, a function name and a class name; the method path should share it rather than grow its own.
- **[thir] Build the async-factory wrapper as a sema-synthesized lambda.** An `async def` referenced as a value at a `Callable` slot returning `Own[@dynamic]` is wrapped by `_async_factory_wrap_cpp` (`tpyc/thir/lower/expressions.py`), which spells the whole C++ closure as a string (`[](<params>) -> <ret> { return ::tpy::make_adapter<Base>(factory(<args>)); }`) and decides each parameter's forwarding itself -- which is how it came to `std::move` a borrowed reference parameter (`BUGS.md#async-factory-wrapper-moves-borrow-param`). The class-name-as-callable path already builds the same kind of thing in sema: a `lambda *a: C(*a)` kept on the name (`TpyName.factory_expansion`, read through `lambda_of`) and lowered by the ordinary lambda arm. The wrapper should be that: a synthesized `lambda *a: f(*a)` whose body RETURN-coerces to `Own[@dynamic]`, so the adapter construction, the parameter spellings and the argument forwarding come from the existing lambda, call and coercion arms, and the string builder goes.
- **[sema] One shape for a class name at a callable slot.** The synthesized `lambda *a: C(*a)` lives on `TpyName.factory_expansion`, and `coerce_expr` swaps it into the tree only where a slot conversion runs (overload resolution calls it only `if arg_t != ptype`), so the same construct reaches THIR either as the name or as the lambda. Consumers go through `lambda_of`, but tree walkers do not: `CaptureSites` (`tpyc/thir/lower/captures.py`) numbers the swapped-in lambda and not the side-field one. Unobservable today (a factory lambda captures nothing). Put the lambda in the tree wherever sema decides it -- every hinted slot already stores back what `coerce_expr` returns -- and drop the side field.
- **[sema] `_names_class` resolves an imported name by qualified name only.** Its import branch still tries short-name lookups (`registry.get_function`, `calls._record_for_local_name`, `registry.get_enum`) before the record `SemanticContext.class_record_of` resolves by the import's qualified name -- the short-name key collides for same-named records across modules. Route it through `class_record_of` plus the enum check.
- Generic Fn param type deduction: `sorted[T,K](Iterable[T], Fn[[T],K])` shares T between iterable and Fn, so the Fn param can widen T (e.g. `sorted([3,1,4], key=negate)` widens T from int32 to BigInt). In C++, T and KeyFn are independent template params -- the key function's type is deduced separately and implicit conversion handles the call. The proper TPy fix: support independent callable type params bounded over other params, e.g. `sorted[T, KFn: Callable[[T], Comparable]](Iterable[T], KFn)`. Current behavior (widening) is correct but suboptimal; explicit `list[int32]` + BigInt key already errors.
- type(); (in future `T = type(x); z = T()`)
- tpy.ctypes.CInt32
- ptr() function? Auto-select Ptr vs Ptr[readonly[T]] based on binding mutability. Needs sema-level magic (mutability not in type, it's in binding context).
- `tpy.unsafe.unsafe_address_of(x) -> int`: return the memory address of an object as an integer. Useful for identity comparison in tests (proving reference semantics vs silent copy). C++ codegen: `reinterpret_cast<uintptr_t>(&x)`.

## Python features
- **[design] Should an unannotated container literal of views infer the owning element type?** `xs = [b.name]` (a view getter), `[s]` for a `StrView` parameter and `[line[1:3] for line in lines]` all infer `list[StrView]` today, and a view-typed element slot admits no source (`BUGS.md#view-element-slot-admits-no-source`), so the everyday spelling rejects and the user must write `xs: list[str] = ...`. A list has its own lifetime, so a list of views is only sound when every source provably outlives it -- a MIR question. Inferring `list[str]` instead (the element copies into an owned string, which for an immutable `str` is unobservable in CPython terms) would make the everyday spelling compile and safe with no lifetime analysis. Questions: does it change the type of programs that compile today (a `list[StrView]` inferred from literals of string LITERALS is static storage and legitimately zero-copy -- keep that); the `bytes` / `BytesView` twin; `Span` elements (not copyable into an owner the same way); dict keys and values, set elements, tuples inside the literal; whether an explicit `list[StrView]` annotation then stays the opt-in for the zero-copy form once MIR can prove it. Raised 2026-09-21 by THIR batch 7.
- **Iterating a tuple (`for b in (b1, b2):`, `for shift in (16, 8, 0):`) -- not supported at all today.** Sema refuses every tuple iterable: `for x in (1, 2, 3):` stops at *Cannot iterate over type tuple[IntLiteral(1), IntLiteral(2), IntLiteral(3)]* and `for b in (b1, b2):` at *Cannot iterate over type tuple[Box, Box]*. This is the everyday Python spelling for "do this to these few things", and for REFERENCE types it is the only one that can alias: a list stores its records inline, so `for b in [b1, b2]: b.bump()` copies `b1` and `b2` under the *copies Box into owned storage* warning and the bumps never reach them (TPy `source 1 2`, CPython `source 2 3`; pinned by `tests/cases/iterators/for_literal_named_elements`). That copy is deliberate and stays -- it is the same rule `l = [b1, b2]` and `l.append(b)` follow, and one position aliasing would be an inconsistent model (user decision 2026-09-21). A tuple passes references, so the tuple spelling is the one the language should point users to; today a user who wants to mutate two objects in a loop has no spelling that works. Design questions when picked up (`/tpy-add-feature`): homogeneous element types only, or a mixed tuple through a common supertype / protocol / union; tuple LITERALS only, or also a tuple-typed name, field, parameter and call result; the render for reference elements (the borrow form of a tuple already holds `T*` per element -- the loop variable must alias, never copy) and for value elements; the loop variable's const-ness from the elements' sources; positions -- generator / `async` frames with a suspension inside the loop, module level, comprehensions and generator expressions over a tuple; and the sibling consumers that take any iterable (`sum`, `min` / `max`, `enumerate`, `zip`, `list(...)`, `in`). Once it lands, the copy warning at a list literal of named reference elements in a `for` head should name the tuple spelling as the remedy. Surfaced 2026-09-21 by THIR batch 7, when a fix made the mutating list-literal loop buildable and its divergence visible.
- **Nested comprehensions** (`[x for row in grid for x in row]`). Rejected today with a clean "Nested comprehensions not yet supported"; the double-`for` form is common enough (flattening, cartesian products) to schedule. Surfaced by /tpy-fuzzy-test (collections), 0.3.0 smoke test.
- **`object` and `type` as annotation types.** `object` errors with "Unknown type: object"; `type` with "'type' cannot be used as a type annotation". This blocks the canonical context-manager `__exit__(self, exc_type: type | None, exc_val: BaseException | None, exc_tb: object | None) -> bool` signature -- users must leave those params unannotated. `object` could map to `Any`; `type`-as-value is gated on the same first-class-class-object work as the `## Open feature gaps` `type()` items. At minimum, document the unannotated `__exit__` workaround. Surfaced by /tpy-fuzzy-test (tplib-advanced), 0.3.0 smoke test.
- Enum name lookup: `Kind["TEXT"]` -> `Kind.TEXT`. CPython uses `EnumMeta.__getitem__` with a string key. C++ codegen: `EnumUtil<Kind>::from_name("TEXT")` (already exists in runtime). Needs subscript support on enum types in sema + codegen.
- properties master
- **[LOW] Async: support recursive inline `await` via an opt-in heap-allocated sub-future.** Self- and mutually-recursive inline `await` (`async def f(n): ... return await f(n-1)`; `ping`/`pong`) are rejected today (`async/error_async_{self,mutual,3cycle}_recursive_await`): an inline await stores the callee coro by value in the awaiter's frame (`std::optional<__coro_callee>`), so a cycle is infinite-size. The cycle is already detected by the topological coro-struct emit (`_emit_async_coro_structs`, `tpyc/codegen_cpp/generator.py`). Supporting recursion means heap-allocating the *cyclic* sub-future edge -- a pointer member (`std::unique_ptr<__coro_callee>` or a `Box[...]`) is fixed-size and works off the forward decl, breaking the cycle; emplace becomes a heap alloc, reads deref through the pointer. Only the back-edge that closes a cycle needs heaping; acyclic awaits stay by-value (zero-alloc preserved). **Allocation must be opt-in / non-silent** (it crosses the `@noalloc` zero-heap invariant; recursion inherently needs heap, like CPython frames). Open design question -- candidate spellings: (a) **`await Box(f(n-1))`** [lead -- reuse the existing `Box[T]` explicit-heap primitive at the exact await site; non-recursive `await f()` stays inline]; (b) a coro-level decorator `@recursive` / `@heap_recursion` [coarser, doesn't mark the alloc site]; (c) a `# tpy: heap_await` directive on the await line. Existing no-new-syntax escape hatch: drive the recursion through a `Task` (`asyncio.create_task` already heap-boxes the coro) -- which the reject diagnostic points to; this feature is the lighter-weight direct form. Runtime caveat: the poll chain nests (`poll(outer)`->`poll(sub)`->...), so deep recursion recurses through C++ `poll()` calls -> stack overflow at large depth (bounded recursion fine). Low priority; Task workaround exists. Needs `/tpy-add-feature` (the spelling is a real design decision). Surfaced by user review of the recursive-await reject.
- Generator: `yield from`, `send()`, `throw()`, `close()`
- Generator: protocol-typed params -- residual gaps. Multi-yield resumable-frame generators/coroutines with a static-protocol param (`def gen(it: Iterable[T])`) are DONE (H4, 2026-06-03): the for-loop iterator frame field is typed against the deduced template arg `T_<pname>` (the captured param), not the abstract concept. Follow-ups remain: (1) a protocol param *aliased into a local* then iterated across a suspension (`xs = it; for x in xs: yield x`) is now DONE for the resumable (multi-yield) path -- sema records a forwarding fact (`TpyFunction.forwarded_locals`) for a single-assignment bare-param alias, the local occupies no frame field, and codegen resolves every use to the captured param via `ctx.generator_storage_name`, reusing its `T_<pname>` deduction (generator: `iterators/gen_proto_param_aliased_local` + method variant; coroutine: `async/async_proto_param_aliased_local`; reassignment still rejected: `iterators/error_gen_proto_param_realiased_local`). Remaining sibling: aliasing an `Own[Awaitable[T]]` param then `await`-ing the alias (`aw = coro_param; await aw`) is moot today -- the await-operand restriction rejects awaiting a bare name (only a direct call / Task / Future / `__poll__` value is accepted), so the forwarding path is unreachable there; revisit if await-of-bare-name is ever supported. The non-param-sourced rejection branch and the alias-of-alias chain (`ys = xs`) are now covered by `iterators/error_gen_proto_param_alias_chain`. (2) `await consume(<collection literal>)` -- awaiting a protocol-param coroutine with a `[...]`/`{...}` literal arg directly -- is cleanly rejected (`async/error_async_await_proto_param_literal`); awaiting a *named* iterable works, and the **workaround now works** (bind the literal to a local first, then await -- `async/async_await_proto_param_local_bind`; the local-collection-in-coro crash that previously blocked it is fixed). The remaining gap is only the direct-literal ergonomic form, which would need the await arg hoisted into a frame field (extending the rvalue-temp await-arg hoist); the materialization target now exists.
- Generator: liveness optimization -- only promote yield-crossing variables to struct fields, keep others as stack locals in `__next__()` (currently all locals are promoted)
- Closures: `std::move_only_function` for `Callable` with `Own[T]` params/returns (design doc says to use it, currently uses `std::function` with rvalue params which works but is incorrect per C++23 semantics)
- Closures: `@noalloc` enforcement (Phase 5) -- `Callable` in `@noalloc` context should be rejected. Currently compiles without error.
- `@noalloc` does not flag heap allocations generally: a plain list literal (`xs = [1, 2, 3]`) and the coroutine erasure-boundary `make_adapter` allocation (create_task args, `-> Own[Cancellable[T]]` factory returns) both compile clean under `@noalloc` (probe-verified 2026-07-03). The Level-1 warn-on-allocation profile is the designed home for making the (signature-declared, deliberately marker-free) erasure-boundary allocations visible on demand -- when profile enforcement is built, include the make_adapter boundary class.
- `in` operator without `__contains__`: warn in `@hotpath`/`@noalloc` contexts. Falls back to O(n) linear iteration (`::tpy::seq_contains` for built-in NativeIterables; a `__contains__`-less user iterable is rejected today, BUGS.md#in-over-user-iterable), which is almost certainly not intended in perf-critical code. Users should define `__contains__` for O(1) lookup or be aware of the cost.
- Closures: method references (`obj.method` as a value) -- needs partial application binding `self`. Currently gives "has no field" error.
- Protocol isinstance in ternary expressions: `x = a.foo() if isinstance(a, P1) else a.bar()` generates a runtime `?:` but both branches must be valid C++ at template instantiation time. Fix: generate an IIFE with `if constexpr` inside, e.g. `[&]() -> T { if constexpr (P1<T_a>) { return a.foo(); } else { return a.bar(); } }()`. This also enables single-line field init in `__init__` (goes into the C++ member initializer list instead of requiring unconditional pre-assignment + reassignment in branches).
- Allow `@runtime_checkable` decorator on protocols (no-op in tpyc, enables CPython compatibility for isinstance checks on user-defined protocols)
- Nested patterns in match/case: `case Box(value=str() as v)` for disambiguating parameterized union members like `Box[str] | Box[int]`. Uses field guards with type sub-patterns -- standard Python match syntax, CPython-compatible.
- allow type annotation to use "" (forward decl)
- **Unpacking a `list` (and any non-tuple sequence).** `a, b, c = line.split("\t")` is rejected with `Cannot unpack non-tuple type Own[list[str]]`; unpacking is tuple-only today. Since `split()` returns a `list`, this hits essentially every line-parsing program, and the workaround is indexing each element. Needs a runtime length check to match CPython's `ValueError: not enough values to unpack` -- which is the design question worth settling first (panic vs raise, and whether a statically-known-length source can elide the check). Surfaced by a downstream port.
- **printf-style `%` formatting on `str` (`str.__mod__`).** `"%.2f" % x` is rejected with `Invalid operand types for '%': str and float`, so every such site must become an f-string. Reported downstream as "the single most common change across all three ports" -- so even though f-strings cover the functionality, the absence is the most frequent source of edits when bringing existing Python over. Scope decision needed: the full `%` mini-language (flags/width/precision/`%s`/`%r`/`%d`/`%f`/`%x`, tuple and dict right operands) or a compile-time-format-string-only subset that lowers to the same machinery f-strings already use. The reject spells an internal type name for a literal operand: `"%d" % (2**62)` fails with `Invalid operand types for '%': str and IntLiteral(4611686018427387904)`.
- **Implicit `return None` when a function falls off the end.** TPy requires a `return` on every path (`'f' can reach the end of the function without returning a value`), which is a reasonable design stance, but Python code routinely relies on the implicit `None` -- two functions in a downstream `adatron` port needed unreachable terminal returns added. Worth deciding explicitly: keep the strictness for annotated non-`None` returns (where falling off the end is nearly always a bug) but allow it where the declared return type includes `None`, which is the shape that actually appears in ported code.

## Documentation
- **[docs] One list of the INTENDED divergences from CPython: `docs/CPYTHON_DIVERGENCES.md`.** Today they are scattered: README's four structural bullets (annotations, `int32` literals, value vs reference types with `Own[T]`, no GC), ~36 inline "acknowledged/declared divergence" notes in `docs/LANGUAGE_FEATURES.md`, and a per-feature section in each design doc (`CLOSURES_CALLABLE_DESIGN.md` X, `DYNAMIC_ATTRS_DESIGN.md`, `EXCEPTION_DESIGN.md`, `MATCH_CASE_DESIGN.md`, `DATETIME_DESIGN.md`, `CONSUMING_ITERATION_DESIGN.md`, the container cliff in `CPYTHON_INTEROP.md`). A reader cannot see in one place what TPy does differently on purpose -- the closure by-value snapshot (a rebind after the capture is invisible to the closure, in sync bodies AND inside a generator/async frame) is the kind of entry nobody knows about until the warning fires. Shape: one bullet per intended divergence -- the trigger, the warning it emits (or "silent, documented only"), the escape hatch, the doc it comes from; the four README items included. UNINTENDED or silent divergences are bugs and stay in `BUGS.md` (their "(silent CPython divergence)" tag), never in this list; a divergence found silent while compiling the list is filed there. Write it in a docs-only branch; keep it current afterwards the way `LANGUAGE_FEATURES.md` is.
- **[LOW] Reconcile isinstance status in FEATURE_ROADMAP / UNION_TYPES_DESIGN.** `docs/FEATURE_ROADMAP.md` (~line 208, ~520) and `docs/UNION_TYPES_DESIGN.md` (~line 52) still list the `isinstance(x, (A, B))` tuple form (and isinstance-on-alias) as "not done" / "design only" -- stale pre-existing drift: the tuple form has long shipped, and the inline-union form (`isinstance(x, A | B)`) plus the union-alias-name rejection now exist too. `LANGUAGE_FEATURES.md` is current; these design docs lag. Surfaced by /tpy-review (docs-sync) of the inline-union isinstance feature.
- language restriction documentation
- `tpy --print-types`: internal modules (`tpy._bootstrap.*`, `tpy._builtins.*`, `tpy._core.*`, `tpy._typing`) are shown as top-level sections because that's where the real class/function bodies live. Users import names like `int32`, `Own`, `Span` from `tpy` (via re-exports in `tpy/__init__.py`), so seeing them under `tpy._core._types` is both noisy and slightly misleading (the import path is "wrong"). Hiding the `_*` modules outright removes visibility of every builtin type -- fix properly requires walking re-export chains: when `tpy/__init__.py` does `from ._core import int32`, attribute `int32` to the `tpy` section (with a note on where it's defined) and hide the underlying `_core/_types` entry. Non-trivial: needs import resolution across the package tree in `tpyc/dump_types.py`.

## Type System
- **[design][ANALYSIS DONE 2026-09-16; implementation is its own branch] A branch-first local is a DECLARATION WITHOUT AN INITIALIZER: one slot verdict per binding, read by every hoist site and the straight-line decl.** Today a local first bound inside a compound statement and read after it is predeclared by a hoist that exists once per statement kind (`if` via `_lower_if_hoist_predecls`, and `while`/`for`/`try`/`with`/`match` through five `_lower_hoist_predecls` call sites in `tpyc/thir/lower/statements.py` and `match.py`), and each hoist consults its own type ladder (`_try_hoist_type_ok`, `_nonvalue_hoist_flavor`, the optional-storage flavours) that enumerates the slot spellings it knows how to predeclare. Every type not on a ladder is a located reject, and because the ladders are six independent enumerations the verdict differs BY POSITION for the eleven cells the analysis below measures -- a reference alias compiles at `while`/`for`/`with` and then fails the C++ build, `Rec | None` compiles straight-line and rejects at every hoist, a record alias in a generator rejects straight-line and compiles branch-first. The batch-5 review filed that branch-first/straight-line split as its own family; the `str | None` half of it is already closed, the straight-line decl having been admitted with the copy the branch-first hoist already took (`tests/cases/optional/view_at_owned_opt_decl`). Two more of the same shape are filed: a union-typed local is on no ladder at all (`BUGS.md#union-local-hoist-unclassified`, every position in a PLAIN body rejecting together since they share the classifier), and the match ladder still refuses reassigned non-value locals and pattern captures in a plain body (`BUGS.md#match-nonvalue-hoist-unadmitted`); ordinary single-binding moves/copies now use the shared storage flavors. The rule: the slot form of a local is decided ONCE per binding, where declarations are decided (the slot-derived-verdicts model already merged for sync declarations), and a hoist is that declaration rendered without an initializer, the arm's assignment then taking the ordinary rebind/reseat path. That deletes the hoist ladders and the per-statement flavour rows, makes every hoist site a reader of one verdict, and closes the position-split entries (`BUGS.md#branch-first-alias-drops-const` at the const cell; the move cell is resolved by `docs/LOCAL_BINDING_LOWERING_PLAN.md`). Snapshot-visible (predecl spellings may change), so it needs the position-by-shape matrix and its own review; the natural continuation of the slot-derived verdicts work. Raised by the user reviewing batch 5 ("why do we have to spell every possible option? this should be generic code"). ANALYSIS (batch 6, measured on 9813ac2a26: 17 type families x 9 positions, 153 probes, both with differing and identical arm sources): `s: StrView | None = a`, the shape this entry was first raised on, now rejects at BOTH positions (`decl.slot_type` straight-line, `if.hoist_type` branch-first, pinned by `tests/cases/optional/error_branch_first_opt_view_inner`), so it is a missing spelling rather than a split. The debt is eleven cells whose verdict differs by position: a reference ALIAS at while/for/with/try-finally compiles and then FAILS THE C++ BUILD (`Rec* v;` against `const Rec&`, `BUGS.md#branch-first-alias-drops-const`, HIGH; the if/try-except twins are well-formed only because two arms binding marks the source parameter mutated, so the ABI depends on arm count); a list alias rejects `decl.reseat_source` at while/for/with where if/try/decl compile; the borrow-tuple rung is wired into if/for/try but not while/with/match; a value union rejects at the isinstance READ straight-line and with but narrows when hoisted; `Rec | None` compiles straight-line and rejects at every hoist (`decl.reseat_param_source`); `list[int32] | None` rejects everywhere under two tags; a record/list alias in a GENERATOR rejects straight-line (`res.alias_bind`) and compiles branch-first; `str | None` in a frame rejects at both (`res.local_storage`, re-verified 2026-09-20); at that baseline every non-value `match` hoist rejected in a PLAIN body (ordinary single-binding moves/copies were subsequently admitted; reassigned/capture forms still reject), while in a resumable one the frame member is the declaration and the same hoist compiles (re-verified 2026-09-20; the other resumable cells above -- the generator alias split, the value-union isinstance read -- are unverified since the 2026-09-16 measurement); `v = Rec()` renders THREE ways across five positions (bare slot / two `__slot_N` optionals + pointer / one optional); `StrView | None` rejects under five tags.
